Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to promoting local food access and employment opportunities is outlined in various policies, including Policy DS1, which sets out the overall development need for Coventry (Coventry Local Plan, Policy DS1) [Source 3]. 
Policy DS2 identifies sites and schemes where cross-boundary cooperation will be important, such as the growth around Whitley Business Park and Ansty Park (Coventry Local Plan Proposed Modifications, Section 6.8) [Source 2]. 
The NPPF requires plan-making authorities to cooperate on cross-boundary infrastructure and optimal locations for growth, including determining optimal locations for growth, such as in connected places for housing or along major transport corridors for some types of employment (NPPF, PM10, paragraph 1c) [Source 1]. 
The Coventry Local Plan demonstrates cooperation between plan-making authorities through its review mechanism, which will be triggered if the Plan does not deliver the homes, jobs, and infrastructure it sets out or if a neighbouring authority is proven to be unable to accommodate Coventry's unmet need (Coventry Local Plan Proposed Modifications, Section 6.8) [Source 2]. 
The Plan also identifies the need for cross-boundary cooperation to address Coventry's unmet need for housing and employment land, stating that it will continue to work actively with neighbouring Councils through the Duty to Cooperate (Coventry Local Plan, Section 1) [Source 3].

Coventry's City Centre Area Action Plan (AAP) designates the Primary Shopping Area (PSA) through the AAP (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 190) (Coventry AAP, Inspector's Report, paragraph 24). The NPPF advises that local planning authorities should define a network and hierarchy of centres that is resilient to anticipated future economic changes (NPPF, as referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 190) (Coventry AAP, Inspector's Report, paragraph 24). Coventry City centre sits at the top of the Council’s centres hierarchy as the main focus for comparison shopping as well as employment, leisure and entertainment (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 190) (Coventry AAP, Inspector's Report, paragraph 24). The hierarchy is set out in LP Policy R3, which identifies Major District Centres (MDCs), District Centres (DCs), and Local Centres (LCs) below the City centre (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 191) (Coventry AAP, Inspector's Report, paragraph 25). The Primary Shopping Area is designated through the AAP, aligning with the NPPF's requirement for local plans to define the location and boundaries of town centres (Coventry AAP, Section 24) (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 190).

- Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report: Coventry City Council Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017 — paragraphs 190, 191

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on providing accessible social infrastructure and adaptable housing is reflected in its policies, such as Policy DS4A, which outlines general masterplan principles for major development proposals (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 55 of 99). These principles include the timely provision of supporting infrastructure and planning proposals in a comprehensive and integrated manner (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 55 of 99). The NPPF requires viability assessments to be carried out to ensure that development proposals are viable and can deliver the required infrastructure and housing (NPPF, paragraph not specified in the provided documents). The Coventry Local Plan's viability assessments, such as the Affordable Housing Economic Viability Assessment, have been used to inform policy requirements, including the affordable housing requirement (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 66). The plan includes flexibility to negotiate on a site-by-site basis, with specific reference to viability in policy wording (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 66). The NPPF requires that plans should be reviewed regularly to ensure they remain effective and viable (NPPF, paragraph not specified in the provided documents). The Coventry Local Plan will be reviewed prior to the end of the Plan Period in the event of certain circumstances arising, including changes to national policy or significant changes to the development strategy (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 24 of 99).

The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD requires applicants to assess and mitigate health impacts in all proposed developments by using a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) or a HIA Screening Report for major development proposals (Coventry Local Plan, Policy HW1; Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). 
The SPD provides guidance on completing a health toolkit, such as the Healthy Developments Template, to identify health impacts and inform design decisions (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
This template is designed to be used early in the planning process to help maximize positive health impacts and minimize adverse ones (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The SPD aims to support the creation of well-designed, attractive, and healthy places by considering the wider determinants of health, including physical and social conditions, and good quality lifestyle choices (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 2). 
The Coventry Local Plan's Policy HW1 reinforces the Government's approach to having health in all policies and enables health implications to be taken into consideration during the decision-making process for development design (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Healthy Development Template process in Coventry's Supplementary Planning Document is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making for a development proposal to have the best possible impact on health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The Healthy Development Template is not designed to create extra work, but to complement a variety of policies contained in the Coventry Local Plan that can impact the wider determinants of health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The National Planning Policy Framework requires that supplementary plans have regard to national policies and guidance issued by the Secretary of State, and not duplicate, substantively restate or modify the content of national policies for decision-making (Draft NPPF, PM16). 
The Healthy Development Template aligns with this requirement by providing a tool that allows existing work to be recorded from a health perspective, and is not intended to duplicate or restate national policies (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The Template considers various categories and criteria that influence health and wellbeing, and allows for extra criteria to be added as necessary for a particular proposed development (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.2). 
Coventry's Local Plan embeds health and wellbeing considerations, as demonstrated by the Health Impact Assessment, which ensures that policies reduce health inequalities and do not actively damage health (LP27 Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 1.8).

The Coventry Hot Food Takeaway Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) addresses national policy guidance on using Article 4 directions by considering the over-concentration and clustering of certain use classes within a specified area (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified). The SPD uses an evidence base that includes studies showing a link between the concentration of hot food takeaways and obesity (Appendix A to the draft HFT SPD, Chapter 1.4). The evidence base also references more recent research, such as Burgoine et al. (2014) and Health Matters: Obesity and the food environment (2017) (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified). The SPD justifies its approach by citing the need to reduce harmful cumulative impacts, including displacement of other retail shops and increased numbers of customers around hot food takeaways (Appendix A to the draft HFT SPD, Section not specified). The SPD also notes that it is part of a city-wide, whole systems approach to childhood obesity and does not seek to resolve childhood obesity as a single measure (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD builds upon the national planning policy's emphasis on liveability and healthy communities by providing a framework for assessing the health impacts of new developments (Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.3). 
This SPD supports the Local Plan's policy themes, including health and wellbeing, green environment, design, communities, retail, and leisure, which aim to promote health and wellbeing (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 3.6). 
The SPD recommends that developers complete a Health Impacts Toolkit or the Healthy Developments Template to identify potential health impacts and mitigation measures (Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The Healthy Developments Template is designed to be used early in the planning process to inform decision-making and ensure that developments have a positive impact on health (Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The SPD also encourages collaboration between the planning department and public health to ensure that health and wellbeing are embedded in future planning policy documents (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.3).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Air Quality Local Plan's emphasis on clearer requirements for air quality monitoring and assessments is outlined in the Air Quality SPD, which states that requirements for monitoring air quality as part of air quality assessments submitted to support planning applications have been made clearer in section 5 and appendix 1 (Coventry Air Quality SPD, Appendix 2, page not specified but mentioned multiple times). 
Major applications will still be required to provide air quality assessments, and these will be used to require bespoke mitigation, which may exceptionally include environmental damage costs to be paid by the developer (Coventry Air Quality SPD, Cabinet Member Report, paragraph 1.3). 
The NPPF's guidance on viability assessments is not directly referenced in the provided documents; however, the Air Quality SPD does mention that the Council will continue to resist inappropriate development proposals in areas where the air quality objective is borderline or already exceeded (Coventry Air Quality SPD, Cabinet Member Report, paragraph 1.3). 
When additional monitoring or mitigation measures may impose unforeseen costs on development proposals, the Air Quality SPD suggests that major developments will be required to undertake full air quality assessments and implement mitigation measures, such as electric vehicle charging points (Coventry Air Quality SPD, Cabinet Member Report, paragraph 1.6). 
The Coventry Local Plan's Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report identifies that large-scale housing and employment development could have a negative effect on air quality as a result of increased vehicle traffic (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, paragraph 7.3).

Coventry's Policy CC22 aims to maintain a high proportion of A1 retail uses in primary frontages, with a clear majority of A1 retail uses expected to remain within all Primary Frontages at all times (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22). 
Where proposals would result in less than 60% of primary frontages being classed as A1 retail, the applicant will be expected to demonstrate exceptional circumstances to justify a change of use (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22). 
Under no circumstances will A1 retail be allowed to fall below 51% of primary frontages (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22). 
Class A5 and sui-generis uses will only be permitted in exceptional circumstances (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22). 
National policy guidance supports the vitality and viability of town centres through plan-making, including setting out the hierarchy of centres and allocating suitable sites in town centres for main town centre uses (NPPF, Policy TC1). 
Local planning authorities are also encouraged to consider the use of Article 4 directions to remove permitted development rights where justified to support the vitality and viability of particular centres (NPPF, paragraph 43). 
Policy CC22 aligns with national policy guidance by maintaining a high proportion of A1 retail uses in primary frontages, thus supporting the vitality and viability of the city centre (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22; NPPF, Policy TC1).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Health Impact Assessment Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) ensures that health impacts are considered in development proposals by requiring applicants to mitigate against potentially significant negative health impacts under Policy HW1 of the Coventry Local Plan (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 1). 
The SPD encourages and recommends the completion of a health toolkit for all development proposals, including those below the threshold in the Coventry Local Plan (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 1). 
The health toolkit is designed to identify potential health impacts and inform the design of a development during the decision-making process (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 1). 
Developers are advised to complete the Healthy Developments Template and submit it with all development applications (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 5). 
The Healthy Developments Template is to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 5). 
The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) requires local planning authorities to work with public health leads and health organisations to understand and take account of the health status and needs of the local population (NPPF, Paragraph 171, as referenced in LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016.pdf, Paragraph 1.6). 
The NPPF's approach to viability assessments is not directly referenced in the provided SPD; however, the SPD's requirement for health impact assessments interacts with the Local Plan's policies, which must be consistent with national policy (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016.pdf, Paragraph 1.4).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) aligns with national policy objectives for supporting clean energy and climate change mitigation in new development by providing guidance on specific areas, such as the University of Warwick campus (University of Warwick SPD, Section 1.1). 
The national planning policy on energy and water infrastructure aims to support the development and operation of energy and water infrastructure in ways that align with wider development, clean power, and net zero objectives (NPPF, paragraph 10). 
The Coventry Local Plan includes policies related to climate change adaptation, renewable energy generation, and air quality, which are consistent with national planning policy (Coventry Local Plan, Policies EM1, EM3, and EM7). 
The Air Quality SPD provides technical guidance and support to Environmental Policy EM7, aiming to reduce the burden on developers and promote electric vehicle use across the city (Air Quality SPD, Section 1.2). 
The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries (University of Warwick SPD, Section 1.4).

Improved social cohesion and social capital can benefit health and wellbeing through the provision of community facilities, areas for play, and increased opportunities for walking and cycling. This is incorporated into several policy themes of the Local Plan including health and wellbeing; green environment; design; communities; retail and leisure. Providing suitable shops and centres for people to meet will help to build social capital, as will supporting accessible community facilities such as schools, healthcare and places of worship. The city centre will continue to be the focus for major community and social facilities which will allow accessibility by public transport and will be enabled by the City Centre Area Action Plan. Public transport will be improved according to the both planning policy documents. This will help those without a car, particularly the young, elderly and mobility impaired, to socialise and interact. In turn this will help to reduce social isolation and improve wellbeing. It may also contribute to reducing pollutants from excessive car trips which impact on air quality. Social cohesion is supported by opportunities within green infrastructure which also includes play areas, school grounds, allotment sites and public realm. These areas will need to be well designed to encourage their use and for increased social capital. In larger office developments, it is recommended that there is provision for social interaction. Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP. 2016 11 6.0 Conclusion and Recommendations 6.1 Coventry’s Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan have the potential to positively influence the health and wellbeing of our population along with a potential to reduce health inequalities. 6.2 The Health Impact Assessment has not highlighted any major impacts on health and wellbeing. Each document incorporates aspects which promote health, and allows for an increased quality of life for the population. 6.3 Clear channels of communication have been maintained between the planning policy team and public health to maintain the standard of planning policies in relation to heath and wellbeing. Coventry’s public health team is keen to continue the collaboration with the planning department to allow for health and wellbeing to be embedded within future planning policy documents. 6.4 The report will be published alongside the proposed Local Plan as part of the public engagement process for consultation and comments invited from a wide range of stakeholders. 6.5 Recommendations  Investigate the possibility of incorporating the Lifetime Homes standard into a proportion of new developments  Consider the integration of physical activity into the design of buildings and social spaces.  Have regard to possible childcare facilities within new developments for education and employment sites  Ensure there is a process for considering the impact of population increase on healthcare facilities  Explore options for including 20mph zones or limits within new residential developments.  Consider the creation of an accessibility standard for fresh food  Agree future projects and work programmes with public health to ensure continued collaboration in line with the National Planning Policy Framework. In this section of the SCI we set out the key documents we need to produce, and how we will engage communities when we produce these. This includes what we must do by law, and what else we will do to ensure that we reflect the local context. We also include a short section on Neighbourhood Plans. This SCI makes provision for this and ensures flexibility to ensure that it can adapt to any future unforeseen circumstances. 1.6 Finally, consultation and engagement often requires the collection of personal data. Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan ensures the provision and enhancement of community facilities in new development areas through several policies, including Policy H3, which requires new housing developments to be located within prescribed distances from public services and facilities, such as medical services and schools (Coventry Local Plan Final Report 2017, paragraph 83). The policy seeks to address any gaps in provision created by new development through appropriate contributions from developers (Coventry Local Plan Final Report 2017, paragraph 84). The City Centre Area Action Plan will continue to be the focus for major community and social facilities, allowing accessibility by public transport (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.0). The Local Plan also incorporates aspects that promote health and wellbeing, including the provision of community facilities, areas for play, and increased opportunities for walking and cycling (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.1).

The national policy's requirements for retaining or replacing key community facilities and public service infrastructure are aligned with the Coventry Local Plan's policies, as the Plan's preparation has been assessed to be consistent with national policy (Coventry Local Plan Final Report 2017, paragraph 1). The National Planning Policy Framework is referenced in the Local Plan's examination, ensuring that the Plan is sound and compliant with national policy (Coventry Local Plan Final Report 2017, paragraph 2). The Local Plan also agrees to future projects and work programmes with public health to ensure continued collaboration in line with the National Planning Policy Framework (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.5).

The Coventry Local Plan's justification for releasing Green Belt land to accommodate housing and employment needs is based on the exceptional circumstances of significant growth anticipated in the area, the City's tight administrative boundaries, and the shortage of available land (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 26). The Plan sets out that the release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified need for housing and employment land, as alternative approaches such as increasing density of development on brownfield land would not provide sufficient capacity (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83). The Coventry Local Plan's approach to allocating development outside settlements is guided by the need to locate development either adjacent to the City's boundary or along key transport corridors to facilitate accessibility to the City (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The Plan's spatial strategy strikes a balance between the three aspects of sustainable development as set out in the NPPF (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 25). The release of Green Belt sites is necessary to maximise housing land provision within Coventry's administrative boundary (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 108).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan's focus on providing new affordable housing aligns with the NPPF's requirement for local plans to allocate sites for development to meet identified housing needs (NPPF, paragraph 23d). The Plan prioritises improvements to the city centre, including residential development, and aims to ensure sufficient housing for elderly people to enable larger housing to be freed up for families (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 17 of 48). The Coventry Local Plan's spatial strategy strikes the appropriate balance between the three aspects of sustainable development as set out in the NPPF, focusing on continued urban regeneration and the sustainable growth of the City (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 25). The Plan promotes sustainable transport modes, including improvements to public transport, cycling, and walking facilities, which aligns with the NPPF's aim to extend transport choice and encourage the use of sustainable modes of transport (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 167; NPPF, paragraph not specified but related to transport). The NPPF requires decisions on development proposals to apply a presumption in favour of sustainable development, which means approving development proposals that accord with an up-to-date development plan without delay (NPPF, Policy S3). 

The Coventry Local Plan's policies, as amended, provide an overarching framework to guide more detailed master planning for transport infrastructure required for strategic sites and links to surrounding areas (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 164). The Plan includes policies to support the delivery of sustainable transport, such as rapid transit and bus services, and to promote walking and cycling (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraphs 164-166).

Coventry's Policy CC9 on drainage and flood risk requires a Flood Risk Assessment to be produced when development occurs, considering the risk of flooding from all sources (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
This assessment must consider the evidence in the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy, Surface Water Management Plan, and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
The policy aligns with national policy requirements, which state that a site-specific flood risk assessment should accompany all development proposals in Flood Zones 2, 3a, and 3b (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 1). 
Additionally, national policy requires site-specific flood risk assessments for development proposals in Flood Zone 1 involving sites of 1 hectare or more, or land identified as having critical drainage problems (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 2). 
Coventry's Policy CC9 also requires new developments to incorporate Sustainable Urban Drainage methods, including treatment for water quality, and to consider the evidence in strategic flood risk assessments (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
The Coventry Local Plan also supports a sequential, risk-based approach to the location of suitable development based on the Environment Agency's latest flood maps, SFRA flood zones, and Vulnerability Classification (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 88 of 99, paragraph 9).

The Coventry Supplementary Planning Documents address the integration of sustainable drainage systems (SuDS) as part of climate change adaptation and the enhancement of green infrastructure in new developments by stating that designing SuDS and other flood alleviation measures can mitigate against potential future flooding through more extreme events caused by climate change (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 6). 
The use of SuDS is also mentioned as a measure to reduce flood risk in new developments (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 6). 
The national planning policy is reflected in the Coventry Local Plan, which requires new developments to address flood risk, apply sustainable drainage systems (SuDS), and manage surface water runoff as close to its source as possible (Coventry Local Plan, Policy EM5, as modified by MM135 and MM136). 
The Coventry Local Plan also emphasizes the importance of green infrastructure in adapting to climate change through the management and enhancement of existing habitats (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Page 36 of 99). 
New development proposals are expected to make provision for green infrastructure to ensure that such development is integrated into the landscape and contributes to improvements in connectivity and public access, biodiversity, landscape conservation, design, archaeology, and recreation (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Page 36 of 99). 
The plan also highlights that Coventry's existing and planned network of green infrastructure should be used as a way of adapting to climate change (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Page 36 of 99).

The process for adopting a Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) in Coventry involves consultation and environmental assessment (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6). The Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012 set out the requirements for producing SPDs, including a minimum statutory public consultation period (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6). Coventry City Council's Statement of Community Involvement sets out a local standard that SPDs should be consulted on for six weeks (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6). The Air Quality SPD, for example, was consulted on for 6 weeks between Monday 7 January 2019 and Monday 18 February 2019 (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, Recommendation 2). 
The Biodiversity Net Gain SPD was adopted by Coventry City Council on 13th December 2022, after consultation took place between 06 July 2022 and 17 August 2022 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD Adoption Statement, paragraph 1). 
It is also a legal requirement to consider whether or not Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) of the SPD should be undertaken (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7). The screening opinion undertaken for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD concluded that no SEA was needed (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7). 
The NPPF defines SPDs as 'documents which add further detail to the development plan' and they are capable of being a material consideration in planning decisions (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1). The Coventry Local Plan provides the framework for determining planning applications, and SPDs provide further guidance on specific issues (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 1.1). 
The Biodiversity Net Gain SPD aims to facilitate the delivery of biodiversity net gain as set out in the Coventry Local Plan and in compliance with national policy (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.2). 
The NPPF's emphasis on safeguarding and enhancing the natural environment is reflected in the Coventry Local Plan's objective to deliver biodiversity enhancement (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.2).

The Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan's Sustainability Appraisal process ensures compliance with national requirements for identifying and evaluating the environmental effects of development by incorporating the requirements for Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) and following government guidance for a staged approach that integrates appraisal to consider the effects of the emerging plan on socio-economic as well as environmental factors (SASEA_Adoption_Statement_Dec_2017, Section 1.1 and 3.1).

The appraisal was carried out by Council officers in workshops with a mix of specialist technical knowledge to rigorously assess potential impacts against the sustainability objectives (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Section 3.3 and 4.2).

matches.text: 1 2 Introduction Coventry enjoys a rich history of architectural innovation and continual development, the city enjoys an environment where markedly different periods of development and associated architectural styles may be experienced in close proximity, thus delivering a highly legible built form narrative to the city. In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Paragraph 130 sets out how planning policy and decisions should ensure that development: a) will function well and add to the overall quality of the area, not just for the short term but over the lifetime of the development; b) are visually attractive as a result of good architecture, layout and appropriate and effective landscaping; c) are sympathetic to local character and history, including the surrounding built environment and landscape setting, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change (such as increased densities); d) establish or maintain a strong sense of place, using the arrangement of streets, spaces, building types and materials to create attractive, welcoming and distinctive places to live, work and visit; e) optimise the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development (including green and other public space) and support local facilities and transport networks; and f) create places that are safe, inclusive and accessible and which promote health and wellbeing, with a high standard of amenity for existing and future users; and where crime and disorder, and the fear of crime, do not undermine the quality of life or community cohesion and resilience. Context (or background) 1.1 The SPD would provide supplementary planning guidance to policy JE1 of the adopted Coventry City Council Local Plan 2011-2031. Policy JE1 (Overall Economy and Employment Strategy) states that ’The Council will work positively and proactively with the business community in the city, inward investors, the City’s two universities, key public sector employers, the CWLEP and neighbouring local authorities to support sustainable economic growth and job creation’, part h of the policy specifically references supporting tourism and visitor related development including the campus and Warwick University, and part i of the policy supports the continued growth of the universities. Policy CO1 (New or improved social, community and leisure premises’), Part 3 states: ‘Where proposals are in accordance with the approved Masterplans for Coventry University or the University of Warwick they will normally be approved subject to high quality design proposals’. There is currently no such Masterplan in place for the area. 1.2 SPD’s are non-statutory documents which can be used to cover a wide range of issues giving detailed guidance on how policies or proposals in the development plan documents will be implemented. Accordingly, they can take the form of a design guide, development brief, masterplan or an issue-based document. The SPD proposed in this report will provide a more detailed masterplan framework as well as the supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus. 1.3 The University’s main campus straddles the administrative boundaries of Coventry and Warwick District, with the majority of the academic faculty buildings being located in Coventry and residential accommodation and sports facilities being largely located within Warwick District. It is important therefore that the SPD is also consistent with Warwick’s relevant Local Plan policy. Furthermore, it should be noted that Warwick are also proposing to adopt the SPD with a report being taken to their Cabinet meeting on 17 October 2024. 1.4 The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries and develop as a Higher Education facility of international importance. 1.5 As the document seeks to clarify the University’s plans for future development on campus and their proposed location, planning consultants Turleys were appointed by the University to lead on the drafting of the document and there has also been input from a range of other consultants. Specific sub-groups were also used to progress certain matters such as ecology and heritage and there was engagement with external bodies including National Highways. The comments shaped the consultation version of the Framework Masterplan SPD. The Coventry Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) on Health Impact Assessment requires consideration of health and community engagement in development proposals, aligning with the national policy's emphasis on creating well-designed, healthy places (Coventry SPD, Section 3.2). The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 emphasizes the importance of good design in bringing about sustainable development and creating better places (Topic Paper Design, Paragraph 2). The NPPF requires that development optimizes the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development, including green and other public space, and supports local facilities and transport networks (NPPF, Paragraph 130e). The Coventry SPD on Health Impact Assessment provides guidance on planning for the built environment to encourage and promote the role of sport and physical activity in creating healthy and sustainable communities (Coventry SPD, Section 3.2). The NPPF promotes the use of tools such as design guides and codes within instruments including local plans and supplementary planning documents to create a framework setting design standards and requirements (Topic Paper Design, Paragraph 128). The Coventry SPD on Health Impact Assessment aims to inform the design of places from a health improvement perspective (Coventry SPD, Section 3.2).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to meeting identified housing needs is based on the objectively assessed need (OAN) for housing in Coventry and Warwickshire, which was identified as 85,440 homes over the Local Plan period of 2011 – 2031 (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 23). Coventry's full OAN over the Plan period is identified as 42,400 or 2,120 homes per annum (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 23). The Plan's housing need assessment was informed by the joint Coventry and Warwickshire Strategic Housing Market Assessment (SHMA), which was updated in 2014 and 2015 to take account of the latest available data (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraphs 21-22). The NPPF requires Local Plans to meet the full, objectively assessed needs for market and affordable housing in the housing market area (NPPF, paragraph 47, as referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 20). The Coventry Local Plan's approach to meeting the needs of specific groups, such as Gypsies and Travellers, involves identifying a need for 29 permanent pitches and 6 temporary or transit pitches (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraphs 92-94). The Plan intends to provide 16 pitches at the Council-owned site once it is refurbished, and 14 pitches are already available in private ownership (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 93). A criteria-based Policy H7 will facilitate the delivery of new windfall sites for permanent pitches over the Plan period (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 93).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to stepped housing delivery trajectories is outlined in Policy H1, which assesses both "Liverpool" and "Sedgefield" approaches to 5-year supply monitoring, as well as a "phased" or stepped trajectory (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 75). The Plan predicts a step up in the annual housing delivery rate from 1,020 to around 1,300 dwellings per year up to 2031, reflecting improving housing market conditions and anticipated completions following the adoption of the Plan (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 76). The release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified housing need, with the Plan proposing the release of parcels of Green Belt land to provide around 7,000 dwellings (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 108). The NPPF emphasizes making efficient use of land and achieving appropriate residential densities, particularly near well-connected transport nodes (NPPF, paragraph 7 and 14; Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 41). The Coventry Local Plan's spatial strategy strikes a balance between sustainable development aspects, focusing on urban regeneration and sustainable growth into greenfield and Green Belt locations (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 103). The Plan's approach to Green Belt release is justified by exceptional circumstances, including the need to meet the housing needs of the Housing Market Area (HMA) and the lack of reasonable alternatives (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 107). The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83; Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 106).

Coventry's approach to defining and allocating retail floor space in its City Centre Area Action Plan aligns with the NPPF's requirement for local planning authorities to plan positively for objectively assessed development needs by identifying a total of 106,834 sq m of gross retail floor space as the total requirement within the wider Coventry area over the Plan period (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 189). The City centre is designated as the main focus for comparison shopping, employment, leisure, and entertainment, and is at the top of the Council's centres hierarchy (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 190). LP Policy R1 sets out that allocations within the City centre would support the provision of at least 70,100 sq m of retail A1 – A5 use, which is clarified by APP/MM13 (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 21). The retail strategy aims to maximise flexibility in terms of how retail space is allocated by grouping retail need within a broader use class range (A1 – A5) (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 192). The NPPF advises that local planning authorities should define a network and hierarchy of centres that is resilient to anticipated future economic changes, which Coventry has done through LP Policy R3 (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 191). The City Centre Area Action Plan contains specific policies that focus on the City centre and designate the Primary Shopping Area (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Inspector's Report, paragraph 24).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to restricting hot food takeaways in specific city centre streets and encouraging healthier food options is outlined in Policy R6, which states that "Outlets should be located in defined centres" (Coventry Local Plan, Policy R6). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides more detailed guidance on this policy, including a restriction on hot food takeaway applications within a 5-minute walk from the gate(s) of any primary or secondary school (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Section 4.2). However, this requirement does not apply to hot food takeaway proposals that fall within a defined centre (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Section 4.2). The NPPF's policy on achieving healthy, inclusive, and safe places is supported by the Coventry Local Plan's approach, as it "aims to achieve healthy, inclusive and safe places" (NPPF, Chapter 8). The NPPF specifically refers to the food environment, stating that planning policies and decisions should "enable and support healthy lifestyles, especially where this would address identified local health and well-being needs – for example through…access to healthier food…" (NPPF, paragraph 91c). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD is consistent with this policy, as it seeks to reduce the negative impact of hot food takeaways on health and wellbeing (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2).

In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan emphasizes integrating green infrastructure and high-quality design to improve air quality, noise, and neighbourhood amenity through policies such as DE1: Ensuring High Quality Design and GE1: Green Infrastructure (Coventry SPD, Section 3.2). The NPPF requires planning policies to ensure development is visually attractive, sympathetic to local character, and creates places that are safe and promote health and wellbeing (NPPF, paragraph 130). The Coventry Local Plan's approach to sustainable development and protecting local amenity aligns with the NPPF's requirements by promoting good design and green infrastructure (Coventry Local Plan Review Evidence Base, Topic Paper Design, Introduction). The NPPF promotes the use of design guides and codes to create a framework setting design standards and requirements (NPPF, paragraph 128). Policy DE1: Ensuring High Quality Design in the Coventry Local Plan sets out criteria for creating high-quality developments that improve the quality of people's lives and are sustainable (Tall Buildings Design Guide and View Management Framework SPD, Section 2.8). The Coventry Local Plan also requires the integration of green infrastructure, which can reduce flood risk, improve air quality, and provide areas for recreation (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Category 4).

Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approaches to improving access to healthy food involve considering public health with regard to the concentration and mix of restaurants, bars, and hot food takeaways (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.5). The plan proposes the development of a supplementary planning document on hot food takeaways to provide guidance on their proliferation, proximity to schools, and controlling densities and concentrations (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.5). The City Centre Area Action Plan has recommended restrictions on hot food takeaways in certain areas due to overconcentration (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.5).

The Coventry Local Plan's approaches to improving employment opportunities include providing a diversity of employment and locating jobs locally to potentially reduce journeys (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.3). The plan aims to maximise opportunities to locate employment within or close to designated centres (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 56 of 99).

The national policy's emphasis on supporting sustainable patterns of movement is aligned with the Coventry Local Plan's policies, which promote housing development close to existing transport links, local centres, and employment (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.4). The plan also encourages the use of public transport, walking, and cycling (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.4).

The national policy's emphasis on mixed-use development is also reflected in the Coventry Local Plan, which encourages mixed-use development and higher density residential development along public transport corridors and in designated centres (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 56 of 99).

The Coventry Local Plan's approaches to improving access to healthy food and employment opportunities align with the national policy's emphasis on supporting sustainable patterns of movement and mixed-use development by promoting development that is accessible by public transport, walking, and cycling, and by encouraging mixed-use development (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Sections 5.4 and 5.5; MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 56 of 99).

The Coventry Supplementary Planning Documents (SPDs) address national policy requirements by providing detailed guidance on specific policies in the Local Plan, rather than duplicating or restating national policies (NPPF, paragraph PM16). 
The Air Quality SPD is intended to support Policy EM7 of the Coventry Local Plan, providing technical guidance on air quality issues (Air Quality SPD, Executive Summary). 
The SPD has been developed in partnership between the Council's Planning, Environmental Protection, and Public Health functions to address health impacts (Air Quality SPD, Executive Summary). 
The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides more detailed guidance for Policy R6 and is supplementary to the Coventry Local Plan, aligning with national policy such as the NPPF in promoting healthy communities (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Consultation Statement, S4.2). 
The SPD's focus on specific local issues, such as the concentration of hot food takeaways near schools, demonstrates consideration of national policies and guidance (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Consultation Statement, S4.2). 
The University of Warwick SPD provides a masterplan framework and supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications, clarifying the University's plans for future development on campus (University of Warwick SPD, Section 1.2).

Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Exp02\nHybrid.answer:
Coventry's approach to addressing health inequalities, particularly in deprived areas, is to work collaboratively with various organisations to create healthy and sustainable communities through planning policy (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 3.2). The city has significant health inequalities, with life expectancy being 11.2 years lower for men and 8.6 years for women in the most deprived areas compared to the least deprived areas (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Paragraph 2.2). The Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan aim to improve health and wellbeing by promoting healthy lifestyles, creating safe and inclusive living environments, and delivering community facilities (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 3.6). This approach is in line with the national policy requirement for residential developments to create well-designed, attractive, and healthy places with efficient use of land, as stated in the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF, Paragraph 130). The NPPF requires that planning policy and decisions ensure development creates places that are safe, inclusive, and accessible, and promote health and wellbeing (NPPF, Paragraph 130). Coventry's Local Plan and supplementary planning documents, such as the Health Impact Assessment SPD, are designed to reduce health inequalities and promote healthy communities (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3).

In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Paragraph 130 sets out how planning policy and decisions should ensure that development: a) will function well and add to the overall quality of the area, not just for the short term but over the lifetime of the development; b) are visually attractive as a result of good architecture, layout and appropriate and effective landscaping; c) are sympathetic to local character and history, including the surrounding built environment and landscape setting, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change (such as increased densities); d) establish or maintain a strong sense of place, using the arrangement of streets, spaces, building types and materials to create attractive, welcoming and distinctive places to live, work and visit; e) optimise the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development (including green and other public space) and support local facilities and transport networks; and f) create places that are safe, inclusive and accessible and which promote health and wellbeing, with a high standard of amenity for existing and future users; and where crime and disorder, and the fear of crime, do not undermine the quality of life or community cohesion and resilience. Exp04b\nFT-BGE v2.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on providing accessible social infrastructure and adaptable housing is reflected in its policies, such as Policy H8, which relates to Care Homes, Supported Housing, Nursing Homes, and Older Persons' accommodation (Coventry Local Plan, Policy H8). The Plan also highlights the importance of social infrastructure, including education, health facilities, and community facilities (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Category 2). The NPPF requires viability assessments to be carried out to ensure that development proposals are viable and can deliver the required infrastructure and housing (NPPF, paragraph 173 is not directly cited but is referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66).

The Coventry Local Plan's viability assessment was updated and monitored to ensure that the evidence base underpinning it remains robust (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). The assessment factored in build standards and infrastructure contributions into a residual value appraisal model (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). Policy H6 includes flexibility to negotiate on a site-by-site basis, and proposed modification MM63 includes specific reference to viability in the policy wording (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66).

The Plan's approach to Green Belt land, including areas that would be removed to accommodate development, is set out in Policy GB1 (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GB1). The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83 is referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 106).

The Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on providing accessible social infrastructure and adaptable housing relates to the NPPF's requirements for viability assessments, as the Plan's policies and viability assessment are designed to ensure that development proposals are viable and can deliver the required infrastructure and housing (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraphs 66 and 103).

The Healthy Development Template process in Coventry's Supplementary Planning Document is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making for a development proposal to have the best possible impact on health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The Healthy Development Template is not designed to create extra work, but to complement a variety of policies contained in the Coventry Local Plan that can impact the wider determinants of health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The National Planning Policy Framework states that supplementary plans should have regard to national policies and guidance issued by the Secretary of State, and should not duplicate, substantively restate or modify the content of national policies for decision-making (Draft NPPF, PM16). 
The Healthy Development Template aligns with this requirement as it is designed to support the implementation of local plan policies, rather than restating national policies (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The Template considers various categories that influence health and wellbeing, including housing quality and design, and is informed by national guidance on health impact assessments (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.2 and Table 1). 
The National Planning Policy Framework promotes healthy communities and considers the wider determinants of health (Draft NPPF, Chapter 8, paragraphs 69-78, as referenced in Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3.1). 
Coventry's Health Impact Assessment SPD references the National Planning Policy Framework and National Planning Practice Guidance, demonstrating regard to national policies (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Sections 3.1 and 3.2).

The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD builds upon the national planning policy's emphasis on liveability and healthy communities by providing a framework for assessing the health impacts of new developments (Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.3). 
It incorporates aspects that promote health and wellbeing, such as providing community facilities, areas for play, and increased opportunities for walking and cycling (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 3.7). 
The SPD recommends that developers complete a Health Impacts Toolkit or the Healthy Developments Template to identify potential health impacts and mitigate negative effects (Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The Healthy Developments Template is designed to be used early in the planning process to inform decision-making and ensure that developments have the best possible impact on health (Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The SPD also encourages the integration of physical activity into the design of buildings and social spaces, and the provision of high-quality sports and recreational facilities (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 3.8).

Developers are advised to complete the Healthy Developments Template and submit it with all development applications (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 5).

The NPPF states that "Local planning authorities should work with public health leads and health organisations to understand and take account of the health status and needs of the local population" (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, paragraph 1.6).

Context (or background) 1.1 The SPD would provide supplementary planning guidance to policy JE1 of the adopted Coventry City Council Local Plan 2011-2031. Policy JE1 (Overall Economy and Employment Strategy) states that ’The Council will work positively and proactively with the business community in the city, inward investors, the City’s two universities, key public sector employers, the CWLEP and neighbouring local authorities to support sustainable economic growth and job creation’, part h of the policy specifically references supporting tourism and visitor related development including the campus and Warwick University, and part i of the policy supports the continued growth of the universities. Policy CO1 (New or improved social, community and leisure premises’), Part 3 states: ‘Where proposals are in accordance with the approved Masterplans for Coventry University or the University of Warwick they will normally be approved subject to high quality design proposals’. There is currently no such Masterplan in place for the area. 1.2 SPD’s are non-statutory documents which can be used to cover a wide range of issues giving detailed guidance on how policies or proposals in the development plan documents will be implemented. Accordingly, they can take the form of a design guide, development brief, masterplan or an issue-based document. The SPD proposed in this report will provide a more detailed masterplan framework as well as the supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus. 1.3 The University’s main campus straddles the administrative boundaries of Coventry and Warwick District, with the majority of the academic faculty buildings being located in Coventry and residential accommodation and sports facilities being largely located within Warwick District. It is important therefore that the SPD is also consistent with Warwick’s relevant Local Plan policy. Furthermore, it should be noted that Warwick are also proposing to adopt the SPD with a report being taken to their Cabinet meeting on 17 October 2024. 1.4 The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries and develop as a Higher Education facility of international importance. 1.5 As the document seeks to clarify the University’s plans for future development on campus and their proposed location, planning consultants Turleys were appointed by the University to lead on the drafting of the document and there has also been input from a range of other consultants. However, officers representing Warwick District Council, Coventry City Council and Warwickshire County Council reviewed various drafts of the SPD via a Steering Group. Specific sub-groups were also used to progress certain matters such as ecology and heritage and there was engagement with external bodies including National Highways. The comments shaped the consultation version of the Framework Masterplan SPD. The Coventry Local Plan's justification for releasing Green Belt land to accommodate housing and employment needs is based on the exceptional circumstances of significant growth anticipated in the area, the City's tight administrative boundaries, and the shortage of available land (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 26). The Plan sets out that the release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified need for housing and employment land, as alternative approaches such as increasing density of development on brownfield land would not provide sufficient capacity (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83). The Coventry Local Plan's approach to allocating development outside settlements is guided by the need to locate development either adjacent to the City's boundary or along key transport corridors to facilitate accessibility to the City (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The Plan's spatial strategy strikes a balance between the three aspects of sustainable development as set out in the NPPF (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 25). The release of Green Belt sites is necessary to maximise housing land provision within Coventry's administrative boundary (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 108). The Coventry and Warwickshire Housing Requirements MOU highlights the importance of connectivity to existing settlements or transport corridors (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107).

Coventry's Policy CC9 on drainage and flood risk requires a Flood Risk Assessment to be produced when development occurs, considering the risk of flooding from all sources (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
This assessment must consider the evidence in the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy, Surface Water Management Plan, and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
The policy aligns with national policy requirements, as outlined in the draft NPPF, which states that a site-specific flood risk assessment should accompany all development proposals in Flood Zones 2, 3a, and 3b (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 1). 
Additionally, the national policy requires site-specific flood risk assessments for development proposals in Flood Zone 1 involving sites of 1 hectare or more, or land identified as having critical drainage problems (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 2). 
Coventry's Policy CC9 also requires new developments to utilise Sustainable Urban Drainage methods and consider the alignment of the River Sherbourne and its tributaries (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104; Coventry_AAP_Final_Report, Paragraph 12). 
The use of strategic flood risk evidence in development proposals is supported by Coventry's Policy CC9, which references the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy, Surface Water Management Plan, and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
A sequential, risk-based approach to the location of suitable development will be undertaken by the Council based on the Environment Agency's latest flood maps, SFRA flood zones, and Vulnerability Classification (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Paragraph 9).

The national planning policy is reflected in the Coventry Local Plan, which requires new developments to address flood risk, apply sustainable drainage systems (SuDS), and manage surface water runoff as close to its source as possible (Coventry Local Plan, Policy EM5, as modified by MM135 and MM136). 
Coventry's existing and planned network of green infrastructure should be used as a way of adapting to climate change through the management and enhancement of existing habitats (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy GE1). 
New development will be expected to maintain the quantity, quality, and functionality of existing green infrastructure, and where quantity is not retained, enhancement to quality is expected (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy GE1). 
The Coventry Local Plan also emphasizes the importance of green infrastructure in adapting to climate change and enhancing biodiversity (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy GE1).

The process for adopting a Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) in Coventry involves a minimum statutory public consultation period of four weeks, as set out in the Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
The Coventry City Council's adopted Statement of Community Involvement sets out a local standard that SPDs should be consulted on for six weeks (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 2; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
Consultation for the Air Quality SPD took place for 6 weeks between Monday 7 January 2019 and Monday 18 February 2019 (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 2). 
Consultation for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD took place between 06 July 2022 to 17 August 2022 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
Consultation for the Tall Buildings SPD took place between 03 August to 14 September 2022 (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
It is also a legal requirement to consider whether or not Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) of the SPD should be undertaken, as set out in the Environmental Assessment of Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004 (SEA Regulations) (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
The screening opinion for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD concluded that no SEA is needed (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7). 
The screening opinion for the Tall Buildings SPD also concluded that no SEA is needed as the SPD elaborates on existing policy (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
The NPPF defines SPDs as ‘documents which add further detail to the policies in the development plan’ (NPPF definition cited in Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.1).

The adoption of SPDs is in line with the NPPF's emphasis on plan-making policies that safeguard and enhance the natural environment, as seen in the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD's objective to deliver biodiversity net gain (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.2).

The Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan's Sustainability Appraisal process ensures compliance with national requirements for identifying and evaluating the environmental effects of development by incorporating the requirements for Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) and being prepared in accordance with Regulation 36 of the Town & Country Planning (Local Development) (England) Regulations 2004, Regulation 16 of the Environmental Assessment of Plans & Programmes Regulations 2004, and Paragraph 165 of the National Planning Policy Framework 2012 (SASEA_Adoption_Statement_Dec_2017, Section 1.1).

The SA process comprises a number of stages designed to comply with the requirements of the SEA Regulations (SASEA_Adoption_Statement_Dec_2017, Section 1.3).

The SA Adoption Statement satisfies the requirements for post-adoption (Stage E) and demonstrates compliance with the requirements of the SEA Regulations (SASEA_Adoption_Statement_Dec_2017, Section 1.3).

The preparation of the Sustainability Appraisal involved two stages: Stage A, the production of a Scoping Report, and Stage B, the production of the Sustainability Appraisal Report and Addendum Report (SASEA_Adoption_Statement_Dec_2017, Section 2.1).

The SA Framework was developed to assess the Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan in a systematic and logical way (SASEA_Adoption_Statement_Dec_2017, Section 2.2).

The SA of the Proposed Modifications to the CCAAP was carried out by Council officers in workshops, with guidance provided to ensure high levels of consistency, and a mix of expertise was sought when selecting members of the appraisal group (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Section 4.2).

The SA considered the inter-relationships and potential cumulative effects of the Proposed Modifications using the same method as described in the Submission SA Report (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Section 4.4).

The SA process was undertaken in accordance with government guidance for a staged approach that integrates appraisal to consider the effects of the emerging plan on socio-economic as well as environmental factors (SASEA_Adoption_Statement_Dec_2017, Section 3.1).

Context (or background) 1.1 The SPD would provide supplementary planning guidance to policy JE1 of the adopted Coventry City Council Local Plan 2011-2031. Policy JE1 (Overall Economy and Employment Strategy) states that ’The Council will work positively and proactively with the business community in the city, inward investors, the City’s two universities, key public sector employers, the CWLEP and neighbouring local authorities to support sustainable economic growth and job creation’, part h of the policy specifically references supporting tourism and visitor related development including the campus and Warwick University, and part i of the policy supports the continued growth of the universities. Policy CO1 (New or improved social, community and leisure premises’), Part 3 states: ‘Where proposals are in accordance with the approved Masterplans for Coventry University or the University of Warwick they will normally be approved subject to high quality design proposals’. There is currently no such Masterplan in place for the area. 1.2 SPD’s are non-statutory documents which can be used to cover a wide range of issues giving detailed guidance on how policies or proposals in the development plan documents will be implemented. Accordingly, they can take the form of a design guide, development brief, masterplan or an issue-based document. The SPD proposed in this report will provide a more detailed masterplan framework as well as the supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus. 1.3 The University’s main campus straddles the administrative boundaries of Coventry and Warwick District, with the majority of the academic faculty buildings being located in Coventry and residential accommodation and sports facilities being largely located within Warwick District. It is important therefore that the SPD is also consistent with Warwick’s relevant Local Plan policy. Furthermore, it should be noted that Warwick are also proposing to adopt the SPD with a report being taken to their Cabinet meeting on 17 October 2024. 1.4 The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries and develop as a Higher Education facility of international importance. 1.5 As the document seeks to clarify the University’s plans for future development on campus and their proposed location, planning consultants Turleys were appointed by the University to lead on the drafting of the document and there has also been input from a range of other consultants. However, officers representing Warwick District Council, Coventry City Council and Warwickshire County Council reviewed various drafts of the SPD via a Steering Group. Specific sub-groups were also used to progress certain matters such as ecology and heritage and there was engagement with external bodies including National Highways. The comments shaped the consultation version of the Framework Masterplan SPD. The local authorities have worked together to support the development of this Joint Strategic Housing Market Assessment (SHMA)1. 1.2 The SHMA considers the need for housing across the HMA and in individual local authority areas over the period to 2031. It considers how many homes are needed; what type of homes are needed – both market and affordable; as well as what housing is needed to meet the needs of specific groups within the population including older people and those with disabilities. The assessment is intended to help inform Local Plans alongside wider evidence. 2 OVERALL HOUSING NEED 2.1 The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF)2 sets out the Government’s planning policies for England. It outlines that in planning for housing, councils must work with neighbouring councils to prepare a Strategic Housing Market Assessment (SHMA) for the housing market area, and must also cooperate to ensure the needs of the housing market area are met. The “Duty to Cooperate” is both a legal requirement, based on the 2011 Localism Act, and a soundness test for plan-making. 2.2 The NPPF outlines that the SHMA should provide an objective assessment of the full need for market and affordable housing within the housing market area (para 159). The SHMA does not set housing targets in itself. It provides an assessment of the future need for housing based on facts and unbiased evidence. Government guidance and advice is explicit that the SHMA itself must not apply constraints to the overall assessment of need, such as environmental constraints or issues related to congestion and local infrastructure. This does not mean that these issues are not important - they are very relevant issues in considering where new development should be located. 2.3 The conclusions of this SHMA have been framed by the Planning Practice Guidance (CLG, March 2013). This outlines that the starting point for assessing housing need is the latest set of household projections published by CLG. These are the 2011-based Interim Household Projections. It sets out that these may require adjustment to take account of the latest evidence and to consider need over longer-term timeframes for strategic planning. This has been done through the SHMA in the development of PROJ 1A which takes into account what the 2011 Census shows regarding population trends (and particularly migration) over the 2001-11 period. 1 Stratford-on-Avon DC were not part of the commissioning group for the Assessment but their area was included within it, and the Council had an involvement as a consultee in its preparation. 2 CLG (2012) National Planning Policy Framework

The Coventry Local Plan's approach to stepped housing delivery trajectories is outlined in Policy H1, which assesses both "Liverpool" and "Sedgefield" approaches to 5-year supply monitoring, as well as a "phased" or stepped trajectory (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 75). The Plan predicts a step up in the annual housing delivery rate from 1,020 to around 1,300 dwellings per year up to 2031, reflecting improving housing market conditions and anticipated completions following the adoption of the Plan and removal of the Green Belt policy constraint (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 76). The release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified housing need, as the City's tight administrative boundaries and shortage of available land mean there are limited alternatives (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The NPPF emphasizes making efficient use of land and achieving appropriate residential densities, particularly near well-connected transport nodes (NPPF, paragraph 11, not directly cited but referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 106). The Coventry Local Plan does not directly address residential densities near transport nodes, but it does highlight the importance of locating development along key transport corridors to facilitate accessibility (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The Plan's approach to Green Belt release is justified by exceptional circumstances, including the need to meet housing and employment needs, and is supported by a comprehensive Green Belt review (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraphs 109 and 111).

The SPD proposed in this report will provide a more detailed masterplan framework as well as the supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus. 1.3 The University’s main campus straddles the administrative boundaries of Coventry and Warwick District, with the majority of the academic faculty buildings being located in Coventry and residential accommodation and sports facilities being largely located within Warwick District.
