The Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on providing accessible social infrastructure and adaptable housing is reflected in its policies, such as Policy H8, which relates to Care Homes, Supported Housing, Nursing Homes, and Older Persons' accommodation (Coventry Local Plan, Policy H8). The Plan also highlights the importance of social infrastructure, including education, health facilities, and community facilities (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Category 2). 

The NPPF requires viability assessments to be carried out to ensure that development proposals are viable and can deliver the required infrastructure and housing (NPPF, paragraph 173 is not directly cited but referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). The Coventry Local Plan's viability assessment was updated and monitored to ensure that the evidence base underpinning it remains robust (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). 

The Plan includes flexibility to negotiate on a site-by-site basis, with proposed modification MM63 to include specific reference to viability in Policy H6 (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). The Affordable Housing Economic Viability Assessment (AHEVA) was used to inform the Plan's affordable housing requirement (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66).

The Coventry Local Plan's approach to viability assessments and its emphasis on providing accessible social infrastructure and adaptable housing are related to the NPPF's requirements (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 103). The Plan's spatial strategy strikes the appropriate balance between the three aspects of sustainable development as set out in the NPPF (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 103).

The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD requires applicants to assess and mitigate health impacts in all proposed developments by using a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) or a HIA Screening Report for major development proposals (Coventry Local Plan, Policy HW1; Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). 
The SPD provides guidance on completing a health toolkit, such as the Healthy Developments Template, to identify health impacts and inform design decisions (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The Healthy Developments Template is designed to be used early in the planning process to help maximize positive health impacts and minimize adverse ones (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The SPD aims to support the creation of well-designed, attractive, and healthy places by considering the wider determinants of health, including physical and social conditions, and good quality lifestyle choices (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 2). 
The Coventry Local Plan's Policy HW1 reinforces the government approach to having health in all policies and enables health implications to be taken into consideration during the decision-making process in development design (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2).

The Healthy Development Template process in Coventry's Supplementary Planning Document is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making for a development proposal to have the best possible impact on health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The Healthy Development Template is not designed to create extra work, but to complement a variety of policies contained in the Coventry Local Plan that can impact the wider determinants of health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) states that supplementary plans should have regard to national policies and guidance issued by the Secretary of State, and should not duplicate, substantively restate or modify the content of national policies for decision-making (Draft NPPF, PM16). 
The Healthy Development Template aligns with this requirement as it is designed to support the implementation of local plan policies, rather than duplicating or restating national policies (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The Template considers various categories that influence health and wellbeing, including housing quality and design, and is informed by national guidance on health impact assessments (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.2 and Table 1). 
The NPPF promotes healthy communities and considers the wider determinants of health, which is reflected in the Healthy Development Template's comprehensive approach to assessing health impacts (Draft NPPF, Chapter 8, paragraphs 69-78, as referenced in Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3.1).

(2014) and Health Matters: Obesity and the food environment (2017) (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified). The SPD also references national guidelines supporting its approach, including Strategies for Encouraging Healthier Out of Home Food Provision (LGA and PHE 2017) and Planning Healthy Weight Environments (TCPA, December 2014) (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified). The evidence base is used to justify the SPD's approach to limiting the proliferation of A5 use classes in identified areas (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified). The SPD measures the concentration of hot food takeaways at the Lower Super Output Area (LSOA) level, as this is the lowest geographical level for which data is available (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified).

The SPD also encourages the integration of physical activity into the design of buildings and social spaces, and the provision of community facilities and healthcare infrastructure (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.5).

Developers are advised to complete the Healthy Developments Template and submit it with all development applications (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 5). 
The Healthy Developments Template is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making and ensure a development proposal has the best possible impact on health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Chapter 5).

The Coventry Local Plan's justification for releasing Green Belt land to accommodate housing and employment needs is based on the exceptional circumstances of significant growth anticipated in the area, the City's tight administrative boundaries, and the shortage of available land (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 26). The Plan sets out that the release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified need for housing and employment land, as alternative approaches such as increasing density of development on brownfield land would not provide sufficient capacity (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83). The Coventry Local Plan's approach to allocating development outside settlements is guided by the need to locate development either adjacent to the City's boundary or along key transport corridors to facilitate accessibility to the City (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The Plan's spatial strategy strikes a balance between the three aspects of sustainable development as set out in the NPPF (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 25). The release of Green Belt sites is necessary to maximise housing land provision within Coventry's administrative boundary (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 108). The Duty to Cooperate requires neighbouring authorities in the Housing Market Area (HMA) to help meet Coventry's shortfall in housing needs (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 108).

Coventry's Policy CC9 on drainage and flood risk requires a Flood Risk Assessment to be produced when development occurs, considering the risk of flooding from all sources (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
The policy also mandates consideration of the evidence in the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy, Surface Water Management Plan, and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
This aligns with national policy requirements, which state that a site-specific flood risk assessment should accompany development proposals in Flood Zones 2, 3a, and 3b, as well as certain developments in Flood Zone 1 (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making). 
The national policy also requires site-specific flood risk assessments to be appropriate to the scale, nature, and location of development (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making). 
Coventry's Policy CC9 further requires new developments to utilise Sustainable Urban Drainage methods and consider the alignment of the River Sherbourne and its tributaries (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104; Coventry_AAP_Final_Report, Paragraph 12). 
The use of strategic flood risk evidence in development proposals is also reflected in Coventry's policy, as it requires consideration of the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
A sequential, risk-based approach to development location is undertaken by the Council based on the Environment Agency's latest flood maps, SFRA flood zones, and Vulnerability Classification (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Paragraph 9).

The process for adopting a Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) in Coventry involves a minimum statutory public consultation period of four weeks, as set out in the Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
The Coventry City Council's adopted Statement of Community Involvement sets out a local standard that SPDs should be consulted on for six weeks (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 2; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
Consultation for the Air Quality SPD took place for 6 weeks between Monday 7 January 2019 and Monday 18 February 2019 (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 2). 
Consultation for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD took place between 06 July 2022 to 17 August 2022 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
Consultation for the Tall Buildings SPD took place between 03 August to 14 September 2022 (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
It is also a legal requirement to consider whether or not Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) of the SPD should be undertaken, as set out in the Environmental Assessment of Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004 (SEA Regulations) (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
The screening opinion for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD concluded that no SEA is needed (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7). 
The screening opinion for the Tall Buildings SPD also concluded that no SEA is needed as the SPD elaborates on existing policy (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
The NPPF defines SPDs as ‘documents which add further detail to the policies in the development plan’ (NPPF definition cited in Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.1). 
SPDs are capable of being a material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.1).

The adoption process for SPDs in Coventry aligns with the NPPF's emphasis on safeguarding and enhancing the natural environment through plan-making policies by providing further guidance on specific issues, such as air quality and biodiversity net gain (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 1.1; Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.2).

The local authorities have worked together to support the development of this Joint Strategic Housing Market Assessment (SHMA)1. 1.2 The SHMA considers the need for housing across the HMA and in individual local authority areas over the period to 2031. It considers how many homes are needed; what type of homes are needed – both market and affordable; as well as what housing is needed to meet the needs of specific groups within the population including older people and those with disabilities. The assessment is intended to help inform Local Plans alongside wider evidence. 2 OVERALL HOUSING NEED 2.1 The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF)2 sets out the Government’s planning policies for England. It outlines that in planning for housing, councils must work with neighbouring councils to prepare a Strategic Housing Market Assessment (SHMA) for the housing market area, and must also cooperate to ensure the needs of the housing market area are met. The “Duty to Cooperate” is both a legal requirement, based on the 2011 Localism Act, and a soundness test for plan-making. 2.2 The NPPF outlines that the SHMA should provide an objective assessment of the full need for market and affordable housing within the housing market area (para 159). The SHMA does not set housing targets in itself. It provides an assessment of the future need for housing based on facts and unbiased evidence. Government guidance and advice is explicit that the SHMA itself must not apply constraints to the overall assessment of need, such as environmental constraints or issues related to congestion and local infrastructure. This does not mean that these issues are not important - they are very relevant issues in considering where new development should be located. 2.3 The conclusions of this SHMA have been framed by the Planning Practice Guidance (CLG, March 2013). This outlines that the starting point for assessing housing need is the latest set of household projections published by CLG. These are the 2011-based Interim Household Projections. It sets out that these may require adjustment to take account of the latest evidence and to consider need over longer-term timeframes for strategic planning. This has been done through the SHMA in the development of PROJ 1A which takes into account what the 2011 Census shows regarding population trends (and particularly migration) over the 2001-11 period. 1 Stratford-on-Avon DC were not part of the commissioning group for the Assessment but their area was included within it, and the Council had an involvement as a consultee in its preparation. 2 CLG (2012) National Planning Policy Framework

The Coventry Local Plan identifies housing needs and sets out measures to meet them in accordance with national planning policy, as required by the NPPF (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, Issue 1). The Plan's objective assessment of housing needs was based on the joint Coventry and Warwickshire SHMA, which was updated in 2013, 2014, and 2015 (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 21). The SHMA identified a full objectively assessed need (OAN) for housing in Coventry of 42,400 homes over the Plan period (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 23). The Council considered the latest available information, including the 2014-based ONS SNPP and DCLG 2014-based household projections, to ensure that the local needs assessments were informed by the most up-to-date data (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 24). The Plan provides for the needs of specific groups, such as Gypsies and Travellers, by identifying a need for 24 permanent caravan pitches and 6 temporary or transit pitches (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 94). The Council will monitor the need for transit accommodation and consider a targeted review of the Plan if necessary (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 95). The distribution of development within Coventry is justified and consistent with the local evidence base and national planning policy, having been informed by the joint SHMA, the Coventry SHLAA, and the SA/SEA process (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 102).

The Coventry Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) uses the Healthy Development Template to assess significant health impacts of development proposals, which includes considering the impact on transport and sustainable movement (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). The Healthy Development Template is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision making (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). The Template considers various criteria, including those related to transport and sustainable movement, such as walking and cycling (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Appendix B). The NPPF requires understanding and addressing the potential impacts of development on transport networks and sustainable movement (NPPF is not directly cited, but the Coventry Connected SPD is mentioned in Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2, and Coventry Local Plan, which is related to NPPF). The Coventry Local Plan Policy HW1 requires Health Impact Assessments for major development proposals, which includes assessing impacts on health and wellbeing (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). The Coventry Connected (Transport) SPD is one of the supporting documents to the Coventry Local Plan that can impact the health of new and existing populations (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2).

The SHLAA identifies the housing supply for the next 5 year period against the equivalent housing requirement. This sets out both the ‘Liverpool’ and ‘Sedgefield’ approaches to 5 year supply monitoring. It has also considered the need for a buffer in line with the NPPF31. The SHLAA assessed a 5% and 20% buffer as well as the impact of a “phased” approach (better described as a stepped trajectory) as set out in Policy H1. It also assessed the 5 year housing supply assuming an “un-phased” (i.e. not stepped) approach. 76. Over the first 5 years of the Plan period, 2011 – 2015, the updated trajectory broadly reflects the amount of housing that has been completed. It is then predicted that there would be a step up in the annual rate, from 1,020 to around 1,300 up to 2031. This is to reflect improving housing market conditions and a predicted uplift in anticipated completions following adoption of the Plan and removal of the Green Belt policy constraint to development of the SUEs. An alternative method would have been to show the trajectory as a flat annual average of the overall housing requirement across the whole plan period. However, to adopt this approach would mean applying a retrospective requirement for the years 2011-2015 which would not accurately reflect the rate of delivery. Furthermore, the stepped trajectory reflects the actual pattern of need which is predicted to increase more rapidly after 2021. 77. The Coventry Local Plan's approach to stepped housing delivery trajectories is outlined in Policy H1, which assesses both "Liverpool" and "Sedgefield" approaches to 5-year supply monitoring, as well as a "phased" or stepped trajectory (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 75). The Plan predicts a step up in the annual housing delivery rate from 1,020 to around 1,300 dwellings per year up to 2031, reflecting improving housing market conditions and anticipated completions following the adoption of the Plan and removal of the Green Belt policy constraint (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 76). The release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified housing need, as the City's tight administrative boundaries and shortage of available land mean there are limited alternatives (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 107). The NPPF emphasizes making efficient use of land and achieving appropriate residential densities, particularly near well-connected transport nodes (NPPF, paragraph 7 and 14; Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 41). The Coventry Local Plan's spatial strategy strikes a balance between sustainable development aspects, focusing on urban regeneration and sustainable growth into greenfield and Green Belt locations (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 103). The Plan's approach to Green Belt release is justified by exceptional circumstances, including the need to meet the housing needs of the Housing Market Area (HMA) and provide employment land to support economic growth (Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 109). The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83; Coventry Local Plan Inspector's Report, paragraph 106).

Coventry's Air Quality Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) supports Local Plan Policy EM7 by providing technical guidance on air quality assessments and mitigation measures for planning applications (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, 1.1). The SPD was developed in partnership with Coventry and Warwickshire authorities, including representatives from planning, environmental health, and public health (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, 1.5). The document sets out guidance for dealing with planning applications where air quality needs to be addressed, including the methodology for identifying development proposals that require air quality assessments (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, 1.6). The SPD also identifies types of development that may require air quality mitigation measures, such as electric vehicle charging points (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, 1.6). The SPD has been developed in accordance with national policy and the West Midlands Low Emissions Towns & Cities Programme (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, 1.4). 

The SPD aligns with the national policy's emphasis on climate and nature by addressing air quality and promoting healthy living environments through planning (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, 1.1). The document requires major applications to provide air quality assessments and implement bespoke mitigation measures to offset potential impacts on local air quality levels (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, 1.3).

The Coventry Local Plan's approach to restricting hot food takeaways in specific city centre streets and encouraging healthier food options is outlined in Policy R6, which states that "Outlets should be located in defined centres" (Coventry Local Plan, Policy R6). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides more detailed guidance on this policy, including the requirement that hot food takeaway applications will not be approved if they fall within a 5-minute walk from the gate(s) of any primary or secondary school, unless they are within a defined centre (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Section 4.2). 
The NPPF's policy on achieving healthy, inclusive, and safe places is outlined in Chapter 8, which states that "planning policies and decisions should aim to achieve healthy, inclusive and safe places" (NPPF, Chapter 8). The NPPF also refers specifically to the food environment, stating that policies should "enable and support healthy lifestyles, especially where this would address identified local health and well-being needs – for example through…access to healthier food…" (NPPF, paragraph 91c). 
The Hot Food Takeaway SPD is consistent with the NPPF's policy, as it seeks to balance the requirements around economy with those around healthy communities (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2, Consultation Statement). The SPD does not seek to restrict all new hot food takeaway applications, but those that are likely to have the greatest negative impact on the health of the community (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2, Consultation Statement).

The SPD proposed in this report will provide a more detailed masterplan framework as well as the supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus. 1.3 The University’s main campus straddles the administrative boundaries of Coventry and Warwick District, with the majority of the academic faculty buildings being located in Coventry and residential accommodation and sports facilities being largely located within Warwick District. Furthermore, it should be noted that Warwick are also proposing to adopt the SPD with a report being taken to their Cabinet meeting on 17 October 2024. 1.4 The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries and develop as a Higher Education facility of international importance. 1.5 As the document seeks to clarify the University’s plans for future development on campus and their proposed location, planning consultants Turleys were appointed by the University to lead on the drafting of the document and there has also been input from a range of other consultants. The Coventry Local Plan's approach to promoting local food access and employment opportunities is addressed through various policies, including those related to healthy food and employment (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment 2016, Section 5.5). The Plan considers the density of hot food takeaways and their impact on obesity, and proposes the development of a supplementary planning document to provide guidance on their proliferation (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment 2016, Section 5.5). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides more detailed guidance on Policy R6 of the Coventry Local Plan, aiming to promote healthy communities and access to healthier food (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2). The NPPF requires plan-making authorities to cooperate on cross-boundary infrastructure and optimal locations for growth, including determining optimal locations for growth such as in connected places for housing or along major transport corridors for some types of employment (NPPF, PM10). The Coventry Local Plan's approach to employment opportunities is considered in more detail within the City Centre Area Action Plan, which aims to provide a diversity of employment and reduce the need for lengthy commutes (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment 2016, Section 5.3). 

The NPPF's requirement for cooperation between plan-making authorities on cross-boundary matters is relevant to Coventry's approach to promoting local food access and employment opportunities, as it involves identifying and addressing cross-boundary matters, including optimal locations for growth (NPPF, PM10). Plan-making authorities should prepare statements of common ground to demonstrate that relevant cross-boundary matters have been addressed (NPPF, PM11).

The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD builds upon the national policy's emphasis on creating well-designed, attractive, and healthy places by requiring applicants to assess and mitigate health impacts in all proposed developments through the use of a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) or a Health Impacts Toolkit (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 1, 4.2, and 5). 
Under Policy HW1 of the Coventry Local Plan, the Council requires applicants to mitigate against potentially significant negative health impacts (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 1). 
The SPD provides information and guidance on completing the relevant health toolkit and the HIA, identifies sources of data to consider, and provides examples of health impacts of the built environment to take into consideration (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 1). 
The Coventry Local Plan encourages and recommends the completion of a health toolkit for all development proposals, including those below the threshold in the Coventry Local Plan (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). 
The Health Impacts Toolkit, or the Healthy Developments Template, is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5 and 5.1). 
The SPD aims to deliver the NHS Five Year Forward View and make health services sustainable for the future by preventing people from becoming ill (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 2).

Exp07\nLLM Graph.answer:
The Healthy Development Template process in Coventry's Supplementary Planning Document is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making for a development proposal to have the best possible impact on health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The Healthy Development Template is not designed to create extra work, but to complement a variety of policies contained in the Coventry Local Plan that can impact the wider determinants of health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The National Planning Policy Framework states that supplementary plans should have regard to national policies and guidance issued by the Secretary of State, and should not duplicate, substantively restate or modify the content of national policies for decision-making (Draft NPPF, PM16). 
The Healthy Development Template aligns with this requirement as it is designed to support the implementation of local plan policies, rather than restating or duplicating national policies (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). 
The Template considers various categories and criteria that influence health and wellbeing, including housing quality and design, and is intended to be used in conjunction with other local plan policies and supplementary planning documents (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.2 and Table 1).

The Coventry Hot Food Takeaway Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) addresses national policy guidance on using Article 4 directions by considering the over-concentration and clustering of certain use classes within a specified area (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified). The SPD uses an evidence base that includes studies showing a link between the concentration of hot food takeaways and obesity (Appendix A to the draft HFT SPD, Chapter 1.4). The evidence base also references more recent research, such as Burgoine et al. (2014) and Health Matters: Obesity and the food environment (2017) (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified). The SPD justifies its approach by citing the need to reduce harmful cumulative impacts, including displacement of other retail shops and increased numbers of customers around hot food takeaways (Appendix A to the draft HFT SPD, Section not specified). The SPD also notes that it is part of a city-wide, whole systems approach to childhood obesity and does not seek to resolve childhood obesity as a single measure (Appendix 2, Consultation Statement, Section not specified).

The SPD also references the Coventry Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan, which incorporate aspects that promote health and wellbeing (Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP, paragraph 6.2). 
The Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan address health inequalities through accessibility to facilities, open and green spaces, social community and leisure facilities (Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP, paragraph 3.8). 
The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD provides guidance on carrying out a Health Impact Assessment, which is a tool used to assess how developments contribute to the health and wellbeing of the local population (Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP, paragraph 4.4).

Exp07\nLLM Graph.answer:
Coventry's Policy CC22 aims to maintain a high proportion of A1 retail uses in primary frontages, with a clear majority of A1 retail uses expected to remain within all Primary Frontages at all times (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22). 
The policy states that where proposals would result in less than 60% of primary frontages being classed as A1 retail, the applicant will be expected to demonstrate exceptional circumstances to justify a change of use (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22). 
Under no circumstances will A1 retail be allowed to fall below 51% of primary frontages (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan, Policy C22). 
National policy guidance supports the vitality and viability of town centres through plan-making, with local planning authorities encouraged to set out the hierarchy of centres and allocate suitable sites in town centres for main town centre uses (NPPF, Policy TC1). 
Local planning authorities are also advised to consider the use of Article 4 directions to remove permitted development rights where justified to support the vitality and viability of particular centres (NPPF, Policy TC1). 
The use of Article 4 directions is not directly mentioned in relation to Coventry's Policy CC22, but it is a national policy tool that can be used to support town centre vitality (NPPF, Policy TC1).

Exp07\nLLM Graph.answer:
The Coventry Health Impact Assessment Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) ensures that health impacts are considered in development proposals by requiring a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) or HIA Screening Report for major development proposals (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). 
Major development proposals are defined as residential developments with 150 or more homes, or site areas of 5 hectares or more, among other criteria (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Schedule 5). 
The HIA or HIA Screening Report is used to demonstrate that the proposed development would have an acceptable impact on health and wellbeing (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Policy HW1). 
For developments that are not considered major, the SPD encourages the use of the Healthy Developments Template to identify potential health impacts (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 6). 
The Healthy Developments Template is designed to be used early in the planning process to inform decision-making and maximize positive health impacts (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 
The NPPF states that "Local planning authorities should work with public health leads and health organisations to understand and take account of the health status and needs of the local population" (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Paragraph 1.6), but it does not directly address how viability assessments interact with health impact considerations. 
The Coventry Local Plan requires that health implications be taken into consideration during the decision-making process for development design (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2).

Context (or background) 1.1 The SPD would provide supplementary planning guidance to policy JE1 of the adopted Coventry City Council Local Plan 2011-2031. Policy JE1 (Overall Economy and Employment Strategy) states that ’The Council will work positively and proactively with the business community in the city, inward investors, the City’s two universities, key public sector employers, the CWLEP and neighbouring local authorities to support sustainable economic growth and job creation’, part h of the policy specifically references supporting tourism and visitor related development including the campus and Warwick University, and part i of the policy supports the continued growth of the universities. Policy CO1 (New or improved social, community and leisure premises’), Part 3 states: ‘Where proposals are in accordance with the approved Masterplans for Coventry University or the University of Warwick they will normally be approved subject to high quality design proposals’. There is currently no such Masterplan in place for the area. 1.2 SPD’s are non-statutory documents which can be used to cover a wide range of issues giving detailed guidance on how policies or proposals in the development plan documents will be implemented. Accordingly, they can take the form of a design guide, development brief, masterplan or an issue-based document. The SPD proposed in this report will provide a more detailed masterplan framework as well as the supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus. 1.3 The University’s main campus straddles the administrative boundaries of Coventry and Warwick District, with the majority of the academic faculty buildings being located in Coventry and residential accommodation and sports facilities being largely located within Warwick District. It is important therefore that the SPD is also consistent with Warwick’s relevant Local Plan policy. Furthermore, it should be noted that Warwick are also proposing to adopt the SPD with a report being taken to their Cabinet meeting on 17 October 2024. 1.4 The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries and develop as a Higher Education facility of international importance. 1.5 As the document seeks to clarify the University’s plans for future development on campus and their proposed location, planning consultants Turleys were appointed by the University to lead on the drafting of the document and there has also been input from a range of other consultants. However, officers representing Warwick District Council, Coventry City Council and Warwickshire County Council reviewed various drafts of the SPD via a Steering Group. Specific sub-groups were also used to progress certain matters such as ecology and heritage and there was engagement with external bodies including National Highways. The comments shaped the consultation version of the Framework Masterplan SPD. The system had to adapt and the law was temporarily changed to enable the planning process to continue, but online. This SCI makes provision for this and ensures flexibility to ensure that it can adapt to any future unforeseen circumstances. 1.6 Finally, consultation and engagement often requires the collection of personal data. The Coventry planning document ensures the provision and enhancement of community facilities in new development areas through several policy themes, including health and wellbeing, green environment, design, and communities (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.0). The city centre will continue to be the focus for major community and social facilities, allowing accessibility by public transport, as enabled by the City Centre Area Action Plan (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, paragraph 3). The Local Plan incorporates aspects that promote health and allow for an increased quality of life for the population (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, paragraph 6.2). Recommendations include investigating the possibility of incorporating childcare facilities within new developments for education and employment sites (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, paragraph 6.5).

The national policy's requirements for retaining or replacing key community facilities and public service infrastructure are outlined in Policy HC6 of the National Planning Policy Framework (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy HC6). Development proposals should not result in the loss of key community facilities and public service infrastructure unless it can be demonstrated that there is no reasonable prospect of the facility being retained or the loss is replaced by equivalent or better provision (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy HC6). The Coventry planning document aligns with this requirement by supporting accessible community facilities such as schools, healthcare, and places of worship (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, paragraph 3).

Exp07\nLLM Graph.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's justification for releasing Green Belt land to accommodate housing and employment needs is based on the exceptional circumstances of significant growth anticipated in the area, the City's tight administrative boundaries, and the shortage of available land (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 26). The Plan sets out that the release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified need for housing and employment land, as alternative approaches such as increasing density of development on brownfield land would not provide sufficient capacity (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83), and the Coventry Local Plan justifies the release of Green Belt land on these grounds (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 106). The Plan also highlights the importance of locating development either adjacent to the City's boundary or along key transport corridors to facilitate accessibility to the City, in line with the Coventry and Warwickshire Housing Requirements MOU (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). The Inspector's Report concludes that the proposed allocations are justified, effective, and consistent with national policy, and that there are exceptional circumstances to justify alterations to the Green Belt boundary (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 149).

- Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017: Coventry_Local_Plan_Final_Report_2017.pdf — paragraphs 26, 106, 107, 149 
- NPPF: National Planning Policy Framework — paragraph 83

The Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan (CCAAP) focuses on providing new affordable housing and promoting sustainable transport modes, which aligns with the NPPF's requirement for local plans to allocate sites for development to meet identified housing and infrastructure needs (CCAAP, Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 26 of 104). The CCAAP promotes new housing growth in the city centre as part of comprehensive mixed-use schemes and at higher densities (CCAAP, Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 26 of 104). It also prioritises improvements to the city centre environment and transport infrastructure, including encouragement of sustainable and active transport modes (CCAAP, Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 26 of 104). The plan aims to avoid out-of-centre development and implement transport infrastructure improvements, such as better-enforced travel plans and improved access for all (CCAAP, Proposed Modifications, March 2017, Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 17 of 48). The NPPF requires local plans to apply a presumption in favour of sustainable development, which is reflected in the CCAAP's objectives to promote sustainable development through mixed-use schemes and sustainable transport (NPPF, paragraph 11). The CCAAP's focus on sustainable development is likely to have a positive impact on the 20 Sustainability Objectives, although it may lead to some negative effects, such as the loss of urban green spaces (CCAAP, Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 26 of 104).

Exp07\nLLM Graph.answer:
Coventry's Policy CC9 on drainage and flood risk requires a Flood Risk Assessment to be produced when development occurs, considering the risk of flooding from all sources (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
This assessment must consider the evidence in the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy, Surface Water Management Plan, and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
The policy aligns with national policy requirements, as outlined in the draft NPPF, which states that a site-specific flood risk assessment should accompany all development proposals in Flood Zones 2, 3a, and 3b (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 1). 
Additionally, the national policy requires site-specific flood risk assessments for development proposals in Flood Zone 1 involving sites of 1 hectare or more, or land identified as having critical drainage problems (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 2). 
Coventry's Policy CC9 also requires new developments to utilise Sustainable Urban Drainage methods and consider the alignment of the River Sherbourne and its tributaries (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104; Coventry_AAP_Final_Report, Paragraph 12). 
The use of strategic flood risk evidence in development proposals is supported by Coventry's Policy CC9, which references the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy, Surface Water Management Plan, and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (AAP5_SASEA_Final_Report_CCAAP_2016, Page 38 of 104). 
A sequential, risk-based approach to the location of suitable development will be undertaken by the Council based on the Environment Agency's latest flood maps, SFRA flood zones, and Vulnerability Classification (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Paragraph 9).

Exp07\nLLM Graph.answer:
The process for adopting a Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) in Coventry involves a minimum statutory public consultation period of four weeks, as set out in the Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
The Coventry City Council's adopted Statement of Community Involvement sets out a local standard that SPDs should be consulted on for six weeks (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 2; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
Consultation for the Air Quality SPD took place for 6 weeks between Monday 7 January 2019 and Monday 18 February 2019 (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 2). 
Consultation for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD took place between 06 July 2022 to 17 August 2022 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
Consultation for the Tall Buildings SPD took place between 03 August to 14 September 2022 (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). 
It is also a legal requirement to consider whether or not Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) of the SPD should be undertaken, as set out in the Environmental Assessment of Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004 (SEA Regulations) (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
The screening opinion for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD concluded that no SEA is needed (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7). 
The screening opinion for the Tall Buildings SPD also concluded that no SEA is needed as the SPD elaborates on existing policy (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6). 
The NPPF defines SPDs as ‘documents which add further detail to the policies in the development plan’ (NPPF definition cited in Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.1). 
SPDs are capable of being a material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.1).

The adoption process for SPDs in Coventry aligns with the NPPF's emphasis on safeguarding and enhancing the natural environment through plan-making policies by providing further guidance on specific issues, such as air quality and biodiversity net gain (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 1.1; Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.2).

matches.text: 1 2 Introduction Coventry enjoys a rich history of architectural innovation and continual development, the city enjoys an environment where markedly different periods of development and associated architectural styles may be experienced in close proximity, thus delivering a highly legible built form narrative to the city. In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Paragraph 130 sets out how planning policy and decisions should ensure that development: a) will function well and add to the overall quality of the area, not just for the short term but over the lifetime of the development; b) are visually attractive as a result of good architecture, layout and appropriate and effective landscaping; c) are sympathetic to local character and history, including the surrounding built environment and landscape setting, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change (such as increased densities); d) establish or maintain a strong sense of place, using the arrangement of streets, spaces, building types and materials to create attractive, welcoming and distinctive places to live, work and visit; e) optimise the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development (including green and other public space) and support local facilities and transport networks; and f) create places that are safe, inclusive and accessible and which promote health and wellbeing, with a high standard of amenity for existing and future users; and where crime and disorder, and the fear of crime, do not undermine the quality of life or community cohesion and resilience. The NPPF further requires that the greatest possible amount of clarity on what is expected with respect to design outcomes and requirements is facilitated as early as possible in the development process (para 128). The NPPF also promotes the use of tools such as design guides and codes within instruments like local plans and supplementary planning documents to create a framework setting design standards and requirements (Topic Paper Design, Paragraph 128). 

The Coventry SPD on Health Impact Assessment and the NPPF both stress the importance of creating healthy and sustainable communities through the design of buildings and places, and the quality of the public realm (Coventry SPD, Section 3.2; NPPF, Paragraph 130f). The NPPF requires that development creates places that are safe, inclusive, and accessible, and promotes health and wellbeing (NPPF, Paragraph 130f).

The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) says that Local Plans should meet the full, objectively assessed needs for market and affordable housing in the housing market area, as far as is consistent with the NPPF’s policies.6 The first step in the process is to identify the full, objectively assessed housing needs. 21. The joint Coventry and Warwickshire (C&W) SHMA was produced on behalf of the Council and its neighbouring authorities in 20137. This was subsequently updated in 20148 and 20159. The C&W joint SHMA identified the Coventry and Warwickshire area as an appropriate housing market area (HMA). The HMA is justified in the C&W joint SHMA report and supported by a national research study by the Centre for Urban and Regional Development Studies which includes parts of all of the Warwickshire authorities as within a Coventry- focussed HMA. Furthermore it is consistent with evidence underpinning the definition of the CWLEP. 22. The starting point for the assessment of housing need was based on the Department of Communities and Local Government (DCLG) household projections, in line with the Planning Practice Guidance (PPG). In 2013 these were based on the 2011-based ‘interim’ household projections and predicted an annual increase in households of 4,066 per annum across the HMA. The Coventry Local Plan identifies housing needs and sets out measures to meet them in accordance with national planning policy, as required by the NPPF (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, Issue 1). The Plan's objectively assessed housing need is based on the joint Coventry and Warwickshire SHMA, which was updated in 2015 to take account of the 2012-based DCLG household projections (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 22). The SHMA identified a full objectively assessed need for housing in Coventry of 42,400 homes over the Plan period (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 23). The Local Plan also provides for the needs of specific groups, such as Gypsies and Travellers, through Policy H7, which allocates sites for Gypsy and Traveller pitches (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 93). The Plan's approach to meeting the needs of Gypsies and Travellers is consistent with national policy, as set out in the PPTS (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 97). The NPPF requires local plans to be produced in accordance with the national framework and use the most up-to-date local housing need figures (NPPF, paragraph 47). The Coventry Local Plan's use of the 2015 SHMA update is considered to be in line with this requirement, as it takes into account the most up-to-date available information at the time (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 24).

The NPPF requires understanding and addressing the potential impacts of development on transport networks and sustainable movement (NPPF is not directly cited, but the Coventry Connected SPD is mentioned in the context, implying a relation to transport; Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). Coventry Local Plan Policy DS3: Sustainable Development Policy and other transport-related policies (AC4: Walking and Cycling, AC5: Bus and Rapid Transport) are relevant to assessing these impacts (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). The Coventry Connected (Transport) SPD is one of the supporting documents to the Coventry Local Plan that can impact the health of new and existing populations (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2).

Policy GB1 sets out the approach to Green Belt land including areas that would be removed from the Green Belt to accommodate development. NPPF paragraph 83 says that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances. The Plan sets out why it is considered that exceptional circumstances exist to justify the release of land from the 41 NPPF paragraphs 7 and 14 42 NPPF paragraphs 159 and 160 43 SHLAA Joint Method Statement (May 2015) Examination Document: LP52 Coventry City Council Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017 26 Green Belt. As outlined above, the evidence shows that significant growth is anticipated for the area. The City’s tight administrative boundaries together with the shortage of available land and diminishing opportunities to develop brownfield sites means that there is a lack of reasonable and appropriate alternatives. There is a need to diversify the housing stock and to meet identified needs for market and affordable housing. Furthermore, there is a need to provide employment land to support planned economic growth. 107. Alternative approaches were considered including increasing density of development on brownfield land and locating development beyond the Green Belt outside of Coventry. However, increasing densities would not provide sufficient capacity to deliver the required housing at the accelerated pace required nor provide adequate opportunities to diversify the housing supply. The Coventry and Warwickshire Housing Requirements MOU highlights the importance of locating development either adjacent to the City’s boundary or along key transport corridors to facilitate accessibility to the City. Seeking to deliver the growth beyond the Green Belt would lead to development located in areas detached from Coventry and increase unsustainable patterns of commuting. It would also have implications in terms of being able to meet the HMA’s housing needs, in particular affordable housing. 108. Unless some of the Green Belt is released, a substantial level of new dwellings -amounting to nearly one third of the planned supply - would not be delivered. The scale of potentially unmet need in the City is exceptional. The selective release of parcels of Green Belt to provide in the region of an additional 7,000 dwellings would make a very substantial contribution towards meeting the shortfall. However, even with the release of the Green Belt and greenfield sites the Plan will leave a shortfall of nearly 18,000 dwellings that will need to be met elsewhere in the wider HMA. This document has been prepared in accordance with the Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012 which requires that Local Authorities set out the persons the local planning authority consulted when preparing the supplementary planning document, a summary of the main issues raised with the consultation responses, and how those issues have been addressed. Once adopted, the Air Quality Supplementary Planning Document will form part of the Council’s Local Plan Background The Air Quality Supplementary Planning Document has been prepared to provide technical guidance and support to Policy EM7 of the new Local Plan. This will help deliver one of the overall objectives of the Plan which is to help improve air quality and wellbeing of Coventry people. The Air Quality Supplementary Planning Document is aimed at individuals and organisations involved in submitting a planning application as well as those involved in the determination and enforcement of planning applications, for all relevant developments (residential, commercial and mixed developments). Public Consultation The Draft Air Quality SPD was approved for public consultation by the Council’s Cabinet Member on 6 August 2018. Notification of the Draft SPD consultation was sent via email and letter to:  Statutory Consultees including adjoining Local Authorities; and  Local Plan database contacts including individuals, developers and community groups. Hard copies of the Draft SPD were made available in the customer contact centre and Council House in the city centre. The consultation was posted on the council’s Facebook and Twitter account as well as appearing on the main council webpages. A number of drop in sessions were also held across the City to facilitate community input and feedback. Comments were requested via email to ldf@coventry.gov.uk. An email address and contact telephone number was provided on all the consultation material and the website for those who wanted to ask questions and seek further information. Summary of Response to the Consultation The Council received a total of 18 responses via email and post as well as a range of informal comments and suggestions made through stakeholder meetings and consultation drop in events. The Coventry Local Plan's approach to restricting hot food takeaways in specific city centre streets and encouraging healthier food options is outlined in Policy R6, which states that "Outlets should be located in defined centres" (Coventry Local Plan, Policy R6). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides more detailed guidance on this policy, including a restriction on hot food takeaway applications within a 5-minute walk from the gate(s) of any primary or secondary school (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Section 4.2). However, this requirement does not apply to hot food takeaway proposals that fall within a defined centre (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Section 4.2). The NPPF's policy on achieving healthy, inclusive, and safe places is supported by the Coventry Local Plan's approach, as it aims to "enable and support healthy lifestyles, especially where this would address identified local health and well-being needs – for example through…access to healthier food…" (NPPF, paragraph 91c). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD is consistent with the NPPF's policy, as it seeks to balance the requirements around economy with those around healthy communities (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2, Consultation Statement). 

The NPPF states that "planning policies and decisions should aim to achieve healthy, inclusive and safe places" (NPPF, Chapter 8). The Coventry Local Plan's Policy R6 establishes the principle of developing a supporting SPD that responds to issues around health and wellbeing (Coventry Local Plan, Policy R6). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides evidence linking obesity to concentration of hot food takeaways (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix A).

matches.text: 1 2 Introduction Coventry enjoys a rich history of architectural innovation and continual development, the city enjoys an environment where markedly different periods of development and associated architectural styles may be experienced in close proximity, thus delivering a highly legible built form narrative to the city. In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Paragraph 130 sets out how planning policy and decisions should ensure that development: a) will function well and add to the overall quality of the area, not just for the short term but over the lifetime of the development; b) are visually attractive as a result of good architecture, layout and appropriate and effective landscaping; c) are sympathetic to local character and history, including the surrounding built environment and landscape setting, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change (such as increased densities); d) establish or maintain a strong sense of place, using the arrangement of streets, spaces, building types and materials to create attractive, welcoming and distinctive places to live, work and visit; e) optimise the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development (including green and other public space) and support local facilities and transport networks; and f) create places that are safe, inclusive and accessible and which promote health and wellbeing, with a high standard of amenity for existing and future users; and where crime and disorder, and the fear of crime, do not undermine the quality of life or community cohesion and resilience. The NPPF further requires that the greatest possible amount of clarity on what is expected with respect to design outcomes and requirements is facilitated as early as possible in the development process (para 128). It promotes the use of tools such as design guides and codes within instruments including local plans and supplementary planning documents to create a 3 framework setting design standards and requirements, with the level of detail or prescription tailored to the specific setting. The Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on integrating green infrastructure and high-quality design is reflected in Policy GE1, which seeks to maintain a strategic network of green and blue spaces (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1, as referenced in Coventry Local Plan Final Report 2017, paragraph 207). This policy aligns with the NPPF's requirements for sustainable development, as the NPPF places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development (Topic Paper Design, Section 2). The NPPF also requires that planning policy and decisions ensure that development is visually attractive, sympathetic to local character and history, and creates places that are safe, inclusive, and accessible (NPPF, paragraph 130). 
The Coventry Local Plan's policies, such as GE1 and DE1, aim to improve air quality, noise, and neighbourhood amenity through the integration of green infrastructure and high-quality design (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Category 4). The NPPF supports this approach by promoting the use of design guides and codes to create a framework setting design standards and requirements (Topic Paper Design, Section 2). 
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to green infrastructure is further detailed in Policy GE1, which requires the maintenance and enhancement of existing green infrastructure, and the creation of new green infrastructure where possible (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1, as referenced in Coventry Local Plan Final Report 2017, paragraph 207). This approach is consistent with the NPPF's requirements for protecting local amenity through plan-making (NPPF, paragraph 130). 
Article 4 directions are not directly referenced in the provided documents; therefore, the specific alignment of the Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on integrating green infrastructure and high-quality design with the NPPF's requirements regarding Article 4 directions cannot be determined (The provided documents do not contain sufficient information to answer this question regarding Article 4 directions).

The Coventry Local Plan's approaches to improving access to healthy food involve considering public health with regard to the concentration and mix of restaurants, bars, and hot food takeaways (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.5). The plan proposes the development of a supplementary planning document on hot food takeaways to provide guidance on their proliferation, proximity to schools, and controlling densities and concentrations (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.5). The City Centre Area Action Plan has recommended that no further hot food takeaways will be permitted on certain streets due to overconcentration (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.5).

The Coventry Local Plan's approaches to improving employment opportunities include providing a diversity of employment and locating jobs locally to potentially reduce journeys (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.4). The plan also emphasizes the importance of mixed-use development and maximizing opportunities for employment and commercial proposals to locate within or close to designated centres (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 55 of 99).

The national policy's emphasis on supporting sustainable patterns of movement is aligned with the Coventry Local Plan's policies on promoting housing development close to existing transport links, local centres, and employment (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.4). The plan also encourages the use of public transport, walking, and cycling, and prioritizes public transport over road use (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 5.4).

The SPD proposed in this report will provide a more detailed masterplan framework as well as the supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus. 1.3 The University’s main campus straddles the administrative boundaries of Coventry and Warwick District, with the majority of the academic faculty buildings being located in Coventry and residential accommodation and sports facilities being largely located within Warwick District. Furthermore, it should be noted that Warwick are also proposing to adopt the SPD with a report being taken to their Cabinet meeting on 17 October 2024. 1.4 The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries and develop as a Higher Education facility of international importance. 1.5 As the document seeks to clarify the University’s plans for future development on campus and their proposed location, planning consultants Turleys were appointed by the University to lead on the drafting of the document and there has also been input from a range of other consultants. The city has significant health inequalities, with men in the most affluent areas living 9.7 years longer than those in the most deprived areas, and women living 8.7 years longer (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Paragraph 3). Coventry became a Marmot City in 2013, embedding the Marmot principles into its core functions to reduce health inequalities and improve health outcomes (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Paragraph 3). The Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan play a crucial role in promoting health and wellbeing by creating safe and inclusive living environments and delivering community facilities (LP27 Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Paragraph 3.6). The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) requires planning policy and decisions to ensure that development creates places that are safe, inclusive, and accessible, and promotes health and wellbeing (Topic Paper Design, Paragraph 2, referencing NPPF paragraph 130).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to promoting local food access and employment opportunities is related to the NPPF's requirement for plan-making authorities to cooperate on cross-boundary infrastructure and optimal locations for growth through its policies on health and wellbeing, employment, and accessibility (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 5). The Local Plan aims to improve health and wellbeing through education, job creation, and retention, and reducing health inequalities over the long term (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 5.3). The Plan also promotes housing development close to existing transport links, local centres, and employment, providing opportunities for social interaction (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 5.4). Additionally, the Local Plan considers access to healthy food and notes an association between the density of hot food takeaways and levels of obesity (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 5.5).

The NPPF requires plan-making authorities to engage proactively and regularly with infrastructure providers, neighbouring and other relevant plan-making authorities to identify and address cross-boundary matters (NPPF, PM10). This includes determining optimal locations for growth, such as along major transport corridors for some types of employment (NPPF, PM10, c). The NPPF also requires plan-making authorities to ensure their plan policies align as fully as possible with those of other bodies where there are strategic interdependencies across boundaries (NPPF, PM10, 2).

The Coventry Local Plan's policies on employment and accessibility are aligned with the NPPF's requirements, as they promote employment opportunities and accessibility through transport links (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 5.3 and 5.4). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides more detailed guidance on Policy R6 of the Coventry Local Plan, which is related to the NPPF's promotion of healthy communities (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2, Section S4.1).

Coventry's City Centre Area Action Plan (AAP) designates the Primary Shopping Area (PSA) through specific policies that focus on the City centre (Coventry AAP Final Report, paragraph 24). The NPPF advises that local planning authorities should define a network and hierarchy of centres that is resilient to anticipated future economic changes (Coventry AAP Final Report, paragraph 24; Coventry Local Plan Final Report, paragraph 190). Coventry City centre sits at the top of the Council's centres hierarchy as the main focus for comparison shopping as well as employment, leisure and entertainment (Coventry AAP Final Report, paragraph 24; Coventry Local Plan Final Report, paragraph 190). The hierarchy is set out in LP Policy R3, which identifies Major District Centres (MDCs), District Centres (DCs), and Local Centres (LCs) below the City centre (Coventry AAP Final Report, paragraph 25; Coventry Local Plan Final Report, paragraph 191). The AAP contains specific policies that focus on the City centre and designate the Primary Shopping Area (Coventry AAP Final Report, paragraph 24). LP Policy R1 sets out that allocations within the City centre would support the provision of at least 70,100 sq m of retail A1 – A5 use (Coventry AAP Final Report, paragraph 21).

References:
- Coventry AAP Final Report — paragraphs 21, 24, 25
- Coventry Local Plan Final Report — paragraphs 190, 191

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on providing accessible social infrastructure and adaptable housing is reflected in its policies, such as Policy DS4A, which requires master plans to identify the timely provision of supporting infrastructure (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 55 of 99). The Plan also highlights the importance of mixed development and protecting green spaces within deprived neighbourhoods to provide opportunities for new facilities (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 55 of 99). 
The NPPF requires viability assessments to be carried out to ensure that development proposals are viable and can deliver the required infrastructure and affordable housing (NPPF is not directly cited but referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). 
The Coventry Local Plan includes policies, such as Policy H6, which requires affordable housing and includes flexibility to negotiate on a site-by-site basis, taking into account viability (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). 
The Plan's affordable housing requirement is based on credible and robust evidence, including the Affordable Housing Economic Viability Assessment (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66). 
The Inspector's Report concludes that the proposed policy requirement for affordable housing is reasonable and that there is evidence to show that since 2012 both build costs and property values have grown, while land values have remained broadly stable (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 66).

However, the provided documents do not directly relate the Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on social infrastructure and adaptable housing to the NPPF's requirements for viability assessments.

Equally the design of buildings and places, and the quality of the public realm are all known to be factors which can have a significant influence on health. 3.3 Planning policy plays an important role in creating healthy communities from the design and provision of infrastructure which supports healthy lifestyles through to the need to provide access to decent housing, sports facilities, recreation, cultural and community facilities and health care facilities. 3.4 When assessing the health impacts of a policy, it is important to take into account the wider determinants as well as the direct determinants of health (such as smoking, diet, alcohol). Some factors are closely under the control of an individual, whereas other factors are not, such as buildings and places. The influence of these social factors of lifestyle choices may explain some of the differences in health seen across Coventry. 3.5 Of critical importance is that the health issues in the city are addressed by policy interventions. The Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan will have a significant influence on the physical development of Coventry over the next 15 years, therefore it is crucial to ensure that development will impact positively on the health of Coventry citizens. 3.6 Through the local development documents, Coventry City Council seeks to improve health and wellbeing by promoting healthy lifestyles, creating safe and inclusive living environments and delivering community facilities which are accessible to services. The policy documents have a key role to promote health and wellbeing. Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD builds upon the national policy's emphasis on creating well-designed, attractive, and healthy places by requiring applicants to assess and mitigate health impacts in all proposed developments through the use of a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) or a Health Impacts Toolkit (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 1, 4.2, and 5). 
Under Policy HW1 of the Coventry Local Plan, major development proposals are required to demonstrate an acceptable impact on health and wellbeing through a HIA or HIA Screening Report (Coventry Local Plan, Policy HW1). 
The SPD provides guidance on completing the relevant health toolkit and HIA, identifying sources of data to consider, and examples of health impacts of the built environment to take into consideration (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 1). 
The Coventry Local Plan encourages and recommends the completion of a health toolkit for all development proposals, including those below the threshold in the Coventry Local Plan (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). 
The Health Impacts Toolkit, or the Healthy Developments Template, is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making and ensure a development proposal has the best possible impact on health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5 and 5.1).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Healthy Development Template process in Coventry's Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) is designed to be used as early as possible in the planning process to help inform decision-making for a development proposal to have the best possible impact on health (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). The Template is an overview of some of the broad determinants that impact health and wellbeing, and is intended to complement a variety of policies contained in the Coventry Local Plan (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). The Template requires consideration of each of the criteria listed in the different categories and completion of the "Details/evidence" column, including those that are not relevant (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). 

The national requirement for supplementary plans is that they must have regard to national policies and guidance issued by the Secretary of State, and not duplicate, substantively restate or modify the content of national policies for decision-making (Draft NPPF, PM16). The Healthy Development Template aligns with this requirement as it is designed to support the implementation of local plan policies and does not duplicate national policies (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5). The Template is also intended to be flexible, allowing extra criteria to be added as necessary for a particular proposed development (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1).

In relation to health and wellbeing considerations in plan-making, the Healthy Development Template is used to identify potential health impacts and recommend mitigations or enhancements (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). This process is consistent with the national policy requirement to have regard to national policies and guidance (Draft NPPF, PM16).
