The respondent also stated that there is a lack of evidence to demonstrate that purchases in fast food outlets are any more or less healthy than purchases in other A Class premises. Coventry City Council acknowledges that hot food takeaway purchases are only one of many contributory factors to childhood obesity. Although unhealthy food is purchased from other A class uses, a significant amount is still purchased from A5 use classes. Appendix A, chapter 1.4, of the draft HFT SPD evidences that the majority of hot food takeaways offer food which is dense and nutritionally poor which, among other health implications, contributes to childhood obesity. The draft HFT SPD is to provide guidance with regard to A5 use class proposals (or those with an element of A5 use class) and therefore does not refer to other A class uses. Coventry does not rule out the opportunity to expand this SPD into other use classes, as appropriate, but at this time the evidence supports a focus on hot food takeaways. In addition, the draft HFT SPD states that the measures are part of a city wide, whole systems approach to childhood obesity and do not seek to resolve childhood obesity as a single measure, but that restricting this one element will positively contribute to the city wide, whole systems approach work on childhood obesity. Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Hot Food Takeaway Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) addresses national policy guidance on using Article 4 directions by considering the over-concentration and clustering of certain use classes within a specified area, as stated in the NPPG (Appendix 2, Section 3). The SPD uses an evidence base that includes data on the concentration of hot food takeaways in Coventry's defined centres, as shown in Figure 6 of Appendix A to the draft HFT SPD (Appendix 4, Figure 6). The evidence base also includes studies that link obesity to the concentration of hot food takeaways (Appendix 4, Appendix A). The SPD justifies its approach by stating that it is supported by an evidence base and is consistent with the NPPG, which allows for local planning authorities to bring forward local plan policies and supplementary planning documents that limit the proliferation of certain use classes in identified areas (Appendix 3, Section 53 of the NPPG). The SPD's approach includes requirements such as not approving hot food takeaway applications within a 5-minute walk from schools, unless they are within a defined centre (Appendix 2, Section 4.2). The SPD also considers the impact of over-concentration on the continuity of retail frontage and the primary retailing function of defined centres (Appendix 4).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Health Impact Assessment SPD builds upon the national planning policy's emphasis on liveability and healthy communities in the design of new developments by incorporating the principles of the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3.1). The NPPF promotes healthy communities and sustainable growth, and includes a section on promoting healthy communities that covers topics such as green space, community cohesion, and education (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3.1). The SPD also aims to reduce health inequalities and improve health outcomes for all, in line with the Marmot principles (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 2). Completing a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) contributes towards meeting the objective of creating and developing healthy and sustainable places and communities (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 2). The SPD recommends considering the integration of physical activity into the design of buildings and social spaces, and exploring options for including 20mph zones or limits within new residential developments (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.5).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Air Quality Local Plan's emphasis on clearer requirements for air quality monitoring and assessments is outlined in the Air Quality SPD, which states that requirements for modelling and monitoring air quality as part of air quality assessments submitted to support planning applications have been made clearer in section 5 and appendix 1 (Air Quality SPD, Appendix 2, Section 5 and Appendix 1). The NPPF's guidance on viability assessments is not directly referenced in the provided documents, but the Air Quality SPD does mention that major applications will be required to provide air quality assessments and may be subject to bespoke mitigation, which may exceptionally include environmental damage costs to be paid by the developer (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft, Paragraph 1.3). The interaction between the two is not explicitly stated, but it is clear that additional monitoring or mitigation measures may impose unforeseen costs on development proposals, as the Air Quality SPD notes that the Council will continue to resist inappropriate development proposals in areas where the air quality objective is borderline or already exceeded (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft, Paragraph 1.3). The Coventry Local Plan's Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report also identifies the need for mitigation measures to improve local air quality, including sustainable transport improvements to be incorporated into new developments (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Section 7.3).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Health Impact Assessment Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) ensures that health impacts are considered in development proposals by requiring major development proposals to demonstrate an acceptable impact on health and wellbeing through a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) or HIA Screening Report (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2; Coventry Local Plan, Policy HW1). 
Major development proposals are defined as residential developments with 150 or more homes or a site area of 5 hectares or more, among other criteria (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Schedule 5). 
The SPD builds upon the health impacts toolkit being developed by Birmingham City Council and is expected to be rolled out across neighbouring authorities within the Health and Wellbeing Alliance (HMA) (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 117). 
The requirement for HIAs interacts with national policy's approach to viability assessments by ensuring that health implications are taken into consideration during the decision-making process for development design (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 4.2). 
The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) states that Local planning authorities should work with public health leads and health organisations to understand and take account of the health status and needs of the local population (NPPF, paragraph 171).

The Coventry Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) provides supplementary planning guidance to policy JE1 of the adopted Coventry City Council Local Plan 2011-2031 (University of Warwick SPD, Section 1.1). Policy JE1 supports sustainable economic growth and job creation, including the growth of the universities (Coventry Local Plan, Policy JE1). The SPD aims to provide a more detailed masterplan framework and supplementary guidance to assist with the determination of future planning applications made in relation to the University of Warwick campus (University of Warwick SPD, Section 1.2). 

The Coventry Local Plan acknowledges the important role of the University in supporting the local economy and the need for the University to be able to grow within its existing boundaries and develop as a Higher Education facility of international importance (University of Warwick SPD, Section 1.4). The SPD addresses the planning policy context and the current campus context by explaining existing land uses and assets (University of Warwick SPD, Section 1.6). 

National policy objectives for supporting clean energy and climate change mitigation in new development are outlined in the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF), which includes policies to support the development and operation of energy and water infrastructure (NPPF, Chapter 10). The NPPF states that the development plan should support the transition to clean power by planning positively for the increased supply and use of renewable and low carbon energy and electricity network infrastructure (NPPF, Policy W2). 

The Coventry Local Plan includes policies related to climate change adaptation (Coventry Local Plan, Policy EM1) and renewable energy generation (Coventry Local Plan, Policy EM3). Policy EM1 relates to planning for climate change adaptation, and changes to the policy refer to the need to seek opportunities to develop new blue infrastructure as appropriate (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, Paragraph 213). Policy EM3 relates to renewable energy generation, and the supporting text clarifies that the policy does not apply to wind energy developments, which will be considered against national policy and guidance (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, Paragraph 214).

The provided documents do not contain sufficient information to directly link the Coventry SPD to national policy objectives for clean energy and climate change mitigation.

Exp08\nCombined.query: How does the Coventry planning document ensure the provision and enhancement of community facilities in new development areas, and how does this align with the national policy's requirements for retaining or replacing key community facilities and public service infrastructure?

matches.text: allows residents to find out more on the future of Coventry’s built environment. Improved social cohesion and social capital can benefit health and wellbeing through the provision of community facilities, areas for play, and increased opportunities for walking and cycling. This is incorporated into several policy themes of the Local Plan including health and wellbeing; green environment; design; communities; retail and leisure. Providing suitable shops and centres for people to meet will help to build social capital, as will supporting accessible community facilities such as schools, healthcare and places of worship. The city centre will continue to be the focus for major community and social facilities which will allow accessibility by public transport and will be enabled by the City Centre Area Action Plan. Public transport will be improved according to the both planning policy documents. This will help those without a car, particularly the young, elderly and mobility impaired, to socialise and interact. In turn this will help to reduce social isolation and improve wellbeing. It may also contribute to reducing pollutants from excessive car trips which impact on air quality. Social cohesion is supported by opportunities within green infrastructure which also includes play areas, school grounds, allotment sites and public realm. These areas will need to be well designed to encourage their use and for increased social capital. In larger office developments, it is recommended that there is provision for social interaction. Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP. 2016 11 6.0 Conclusion and Recommendations 6.1 Coventry’s Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan have the potential to positively influence the health and wellbeing of our population along with a potential to reduce health inequalities. 6.2 The Health Impact Assessment has not highlighted any major impacts on health and wellbeing. Each document incorporates aspects which promote health, and allows for an increased quality of life for the population. 6.3 Clear channels of communication have been maintained between the planning policy team and public health to maintain the standard of planning policies in relation to heath and wellbeing. Coventry’s public health team is keen to continue the collaboration with the planning department to allow for health and wellbeing to be embedded within future planning policy documents. 6.4 The report will be published alongside the proposed Local Plan as part of the public engagement process for consultation and comments invited from a wide range of stakeholders. 6.5 Recommendations  Investigate the possibility of incorporating the Lifetime Homes standard into a proportion of new developments  Consider the integration of physical activity into the design of buildings and social spaces.  Have regard to possible childcare facilities within new developments for education and employment sites  Ensure there is a process for considering the impact of population increase on healthcare facilities  Explore options for including 20mph zones or limits within new residential developments.  Consider the creation of an accessibility standard for fresh food  Agree future projects and work programmes with public health to ensure continued collaboration in line with the National Planning Policy Framework. The SCI has to be kept up to date. This version replaces the previous version which was adopted in 2012. 1.2 The SCI focuses upon the two key elements of the planning process: Planning Policy and Development Management. 1.3 Planning policy sets out the strategic context within which planning applications are considered. In this section of the SCI we set out the key documents we need to produce, and how we will engage communities when we produce these. This includes what we must do by law, and what else we will do to ensure that we reflect the local context. We also include a short section on Neighbourhood Plans. The City Council does not produce these itself but is required to support their production, so we set out what we will do. 1.4 The SCI then looks at the Development Management side of the process. This includes pre-applications (where advice can be requested to guide the production of a planning application or to give an idea of its likelihood of approval), the planning application process itself and how and when decisions are published. 1.5 We also consider resilience. The COVID-19 pandemic meant that many adopted SCIs could not be complied with fully because consultation processes depended upon events being attended in person and hard copies of documents being placed in libraries and so on. The system had to adapt and the law was temporarily changed to enable the planning process to continue, but online. This SCI makes provision for this and ensures flexibility to ensure that it can adapt to any future unforeseen circumstances. 1.6 Finally, consultation and engagement often requires the collection of personal data. We keep this to a minimum, but we handle and manage data in compliance with data protection law. You can find out more in Chapter 5. Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan ensures the provision and enhancement of community facilities in new development areas through several policy themes, including health and wellbeing, green environment, design, and communities (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.0). The city centre will continue to be the focus for major community and social facilities, allowing accessibility by public transport (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.0). The plan recommends investigating the possibility of incorporating childcare facilities within new developments for education and employment sites (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.5). 

The national policy requires that proposals for new development should be informed by an understanding of the need for associated improvements to community facilities and public service infrastructure (Draft NPPF, HC3). Development proposals should not result in the loss of key community facilities and public service infrastructure unless it can be demonstrated that there is no reasonable prospect of the facility being retained or the loss is replaced by equivalent or better provision (Draft NPPF, HC6). 

The Coventry Local Plan aligns with the national policy's requirements by ensuring that new developments provide for community facilities and improvements to public service infrastructure (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.5; Draft NPPF, HC3). The plan's recommendations, such as investigating childcare facilities within new developments, demonstrate this alignment (LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016, Section 6.5).

References:
- LP27_Local_Plan_Health_Impact_Assessment_2016: Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP — Section 6.0, Section 6.5
- Draft NPPF: Draft National Planning Policy Framework — HC3, HC6

The Coventry Local Plan's justification for releasing Green Belt land to accommodate housing and employment needs is based on the exceptional circumstances of significant growth anticipated for the area, the City's tight administrative boundaries, and the shortage of available land and diminishing opportunities to develop brownfield sites (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 26). 
The NPPF requires that alterations to Green Belt boundaries should only be made in exceptional circumstances (NPPF, paragraph 83, as referenced in Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 106). 
The Coventry Local Plan justifies the release of Green Belt land by citing the need to diversify the housing stock and meet identified needs for market and affordable housing, as well as the need to provide employment land to support planned economic growth (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). 
The Plan considered alternative approaches, including increasing density of development on brownfield land and locating development beyond the Green Belt outside of Coventry, but concluded that these alternatives would not provide sufficient capacity or diversity in housing supply and would lead to unsustainable patterns of commuting (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). 
The Coventry and Warwickshire Housing Requirements MOU highlights the importance of locating development either adjacent to the City’s boundary or along key transport corridors to facilitate accessibility to the City (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 107). 
Releasing Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified housing need within Coventry's administrative boundary, as required by the Duty to Cooperate (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 108). 
The release of Green Belt sites is considered necessary to maximise housing land provision within Coventry's administrative boundary (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 108).

References:
- Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017 — paragraphs 26, 106, 107, 108 
- NPPF — paragraph 83

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan (CCAAP) focuses on providing new affordable housing and promoting sustainable transport modes by adopting policy approaches such as new housing growth in the city centre as part of comprehensive mixed-use schemes and prioritising improvements to the city centre environment (CCAAP Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, Page 26 of 104). The CCAAP also aims to implement transport infrastructure improvements, including better-enforced travel plans and encouragement of sustainable and active transport (CCAAP Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, Page 26 of 104). 
The NPPF requires local plans to allocate sites for development to meet identified housing and infrastructure needs while applying a presumption in favour of sustainable development (NPPF, paragraph 11 is not available in the provided context, but it is mentioned in the context that Para 155 of the NPPF is clear on certain points). 
Para 155 of the NPPF states that local planning authorities should seek opportunities to achieve each of the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of sustainable development (CCAAP Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, Paragraph 5.2). 
The CCAAP's focus on mixed-use schemes, higher density development, and sustainable transport aligns with the NPPF's requirement for sustainable development (CCAAP Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, Page 26 of 104). 
The Sustainability Appraisal of the CCAAP indicates that the plan is likely to have a positive impact on sustainability objectives, including housing and community objectives (Coventry Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan – Adoption Statement 2017, Paragraph 3.8).

References:
- [Source 1]: CCAAP Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report — Page 26 of 104
- [Source 2]: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan – Adoption Statement 2017 — Paragraph 3.8
- [Source 4]: CCAAP Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report — Paragraph 5.2

Coventry's Policy CC9 on drainage and flood risk requires development to be designed and located to minimise the risk of flooding and be resilient to flooding (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 27 of 48). 
A Flood Risk Assessment will need to be produced to appropriately consider the risk of flooding from all sources when development occurs (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 38 of 104). 
When development occurs, it must consider the evidence in the Local Flood Risk Management Strategy, Surface Water Management Plan, and Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 38 of 104). 
This includes treating all sites as Greenfield sites when calculating permissible discharge rates (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 38 of 104). 
National policy requires a site-specific flood risk assessment to accompany development proposals in Flood Zones 2, 3a, and 3b (Draft NPPF, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 1). 
In Flood Zone 1, a site-specific flood risk assessment is required for sites of 1 hectare or more, or land identified as having critical drainage problems or increased flood risk (Draft NPPF, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making, paragraph 2). 
Coventry's Policy CC9 aligns with national policy by requiring site-specific flood risk assessments and considering strategic flood risk evidence (Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 38 of 104; Draft NPPF, Policy F4: Assessing flood risk for decision-making).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Supplementary Planning Documents address the integration of sustainable drainage systems (SuDS) as part of climate change adaptation and the enhancement of green infrastructure in new developments by stating that designing SuDS and other flood alleviation measures can mitigate against potential future flooding through more extreme events caused by climate change (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 6). 
New development proposals should make provision for green infrastructure to ensure that such development is integrated into the landscape and contributes to improvements in connectivity and public access, biodiversity, landscape conservation, design, archaeology, and recreation (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1). 
Coventry's existing and planned network of green infrastructure should be used as a way of adapting to climate change through the management and enhancement of existing habitats (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1). 
Policy EM5 of the Coventry Local Plan requires that all development must address flood risk from new developments, apply sustainable drainage systems (SuDS), and ensure that surface water runoff is managed as close to its source as possible (Coventry Local Plan, Policy EM5). 
The national planning policy addresses the integration of SuDS as part of climate change adaptation, and it is necessary to amend local policies to be consistent with national policy (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, Paragraph 216).

The process for adopting a Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) in Coventry involves a minimum statutory public consultation period of four weeks, as set out in the Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). The Coventry City Council's adopted Statement of Community Involvement sets out a local standard that SPDs should be consulted on for six weeks (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5). The consultation period for the Air Quality SPD was proposed to run for 6 weeks between Monday 7 January 2019 and Monday 18 February 2019 (Air Quality SPD, paragraph 2). The Biodiversity Net Gain SPD was consulted on between 06 July 2022 to 17 August 2022 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.6). The Tall Buildings SPD was consulted on between 03 August to 14 September 2022 (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.5).

It is also a legal requirement to consider whether or not Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) of the SPD should be undertaken, as set out in the Environmental Assessment of Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004 (SEA Regulations) (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7; Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6). The screening opinion undertaken for the Biodiversity Net Gain SPD concludes that no SEA is needed (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.7). The screening opinion undertaken for the Tall Buildings SPD also concludes that no SEA is needed as the SPD elaborates on existing policy (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.6).

The NPPF defines SPDs as ‘documents which add further detail to the policies in the development plan’ (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.1; Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1). SPDs are capable of being a material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan (Tall Buildings SPD, paragraph 1.1; Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1).

The NPPF's emphasis on safeguarding and enhancing the natural environment through plan-making policies is reflected in the Coventry Local Plan and its supporting SPDs (NPPF is referenced in Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.1). The Biodiversity Net Gain SPD aims to facilitate the delivery of biodiversity net gain as set out in the Coventry Local Plan and in compliance with the most up-to-date national policy as set out in the Environment Act 2021 (Biodiversity Net Gain SPD, paragraph 1.2).

matches.text: 1 2 Introduction Coventry enjoys a rich history of architectural innovation and continual development, the city enjoys an environment where markedly different periods of development and associated architectural styles may be experienced in close proximity, thus delivering a highly legible built form narrative to the city. In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Paragraph 130 sets out how planning policy and decisions should ensure that development: a) will function well and add to the overall quality of the area, not just for the short term but over the lifetime of the development; b) are visually attractive as a result of good architecture, layout and appropriate and effective landscaping; c) are sympathetic to local character and history, including the surrounding built environment and landscape setting, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change (such as increased densities); d) establish or maintain a strong sense of place, using the arrangement of streets, spaces, building types and materials to create attractive, welcoming and distinctive places to live, work and visit; e) optimise the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development (including green and other public space) and support local facilities and transport networks; and f) create places that are safe, inclusive and accessible and which promote health and wellbeing, with a high standard of amenity for existing and future users; and where crime and disorder, and the fear of crime, do not undermine the quality of life or community cohesion and resilience. The NPPF further requires that the greatest possible amount of clarity on what is expected with respect to design outcomes and requirements is facilitated as early as possible in the development process (para 128). The Coventry Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) on Health Impact Assessment requires considering health and community engagement in development proposals to promote healthy lifestyles and create safe and inclusive living environments (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3) [Source 4]. 
The SPD aims to reduce health inequalities by ensuring that planning fully considers the impact on the health of the population (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3) [Source 4]. 
The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) emphasizes creating well-designed, healthy places and optimizing development densities (NPPF, paragraph 130) [Source 1]. 
The NPPF requires that development optimizes the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development, including green and other public space, and support local facilities and transport networks (NPPF, paragraph 130e) [Source 1]. 
The NPPF also promotes the use of tools such as design guides and codes to create a framework setting design standards and requirements (NPPF, paragraph 128) [Source 1]. 
The Coventry SPD on Health Impact Assessment relates to the national policy's emphasis by requiring development proposals to be designed with consideration for health and wellbeing, and by promoting community engagement in the design process (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 3) [Source 4].

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to meeting identified housing needs is based on the joint Coventry and Warwickshire (C&W) Strategic Housing Market Assessment (SHMA), which identified the Coventry and Warwickshire area as an appropriate housing market area (HMA) (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 21). The C&W SHMA was produced in 2013 and updated in 2014 and 2015 to take account of the latest available data, including the Department of Communities and Local Government (DCLG) household projections and Sub National Population Projections (SNPP) (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 22). The SHMA identified a full objectively assessed need (OAN) for housing in Coventry and Warwickshire of 85,440 homes over the Local Plan period of 2011 – 2031 (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 23). Coventry's full OAN over the Plan period is identified as 42,400 or 2,120 homes per annum (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 23). The Local Plan's housing need assessment is consistent with the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) requirement to meet the full, objectively assessed needs for market and affordable housing in the HMA (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 20). The NPPF requires local plans to be produced in accordance with the national framework and use the most up-to-date local housing need figures (NPPF, paragraph 47). The Inspector's report notes that the Council considered the latest available information, including the 2014-based ONS SNPP and DCLG 2014-based household projections, to ensure that the local needs assessments were informed by the most up-to-date data (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 24). The Local Plan also includes provision for specific groups, such as Gypsies and Travellers, with the Inspector's report recommending Main Modifications to provide sites to meet their identified needs (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, Non-Technical Summary).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) uses the Healthy Development Template to assess significant health impacts of development proposals, including those related to transport and sustainable movement (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). The Healthy Development Template considers various categories, including "Sustainable transport" (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Table 1). The Template requires developers to identify relevant criteria, investigate them in depth, and assess potential health impacts, including those related to transport (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). The NPPF requires understanding and addressing the potential impacts of development on transport networks and sustainable movement (NPPF is not directly cited, but the SPD references policies that align with NPPF principles, such as AC3: Demand Management, AC4: Walking and Cycling, AC5: Bus and Rapid Transport) (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Table 1). The Coventry Local Plan policies, such as AC3, AC4, and AC5, are referenced in the SPD as relevant to assessing health impacts related to transport (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Table 1).

The Healthy Development Template is designed to be used early in the planning process to inform decision-making and mitigate potential negative health impacts (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5.1). The Template is intended to complement existing policies in the Coventry Local Plan, including those related to transport and sustainable movement (Health Impact Assessment SPD, Section 5).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to stepped housing delivery trajectories is outlined in Policy H1, which sets out a phased approach to housing land release (Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report, paragraph 72). The Plan anticipates a step up in the annual housing delivery rate from 1,020 to around 1,300 up to 2031, reflecting improving housing market conditions and the removal of Green Belt policy constraints (Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report, paragraph 76). The release of Green Belt land is necessary to meet the identified housing need, with the Plan proposing the removal of certain areas from the Green Belt to accommodate development (Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report, paragraph 106). The NPPF emphasizes the need to make efficient use of land and achieve appropriate residential densities, particularly near well-connected transport nodes (NPPF, paragraph 7 and 14; Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report, paragraph 41). The Coventry Local Plan's spatial strategy strikes a balance between sustainable development aspects, including urban regeneration and sustainable growth into greenfield and Green Belt locations (Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report, paragraph 103). The Plan's approach to Green Belt release is justified by exceptional circumstances, including the need to meet housing and employment needs (Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report, paragraph 107). The SHLAA assessed different approaches to 5-year housing supply monitoring, including stepped and un-phased trajectories, and demonstrated that a stepped trajectory would provide a sufficient supply (Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report, paragraph 75 and 77).

- NPPF — paragraphs 7 and 14

Coventry's approach to defining and allocating retail floor space in its City Centre Area Action Plan (AAP) aligns with the NPPF's requirement by defining a network and hierarchy of centres that is resilient to anticipated future economic changes (NPPF, paragraph 23) (Coventry AAP, paragraph 24). Coventry City centre is at the top of the Council's centres hierarchy as the main focus for comparison shopping, employment, leisure, and entertainment (Coventry AAP, paragraph 24). The AAP contains specific policies focusing on the City centre, including the designation of the Primary Shopping Area (PSA) (Coventry AAP, paragraph 24). The hierarchy is set out in LP Policy R3, identifying Major District Centres (MDCs), District Centres (DCs), and Local Centres (LCs) below the City centre (Coventry Local Plan, Policy R3) (Coventry AAP, paragraph 25). LP Policy R1 sets out that allocations within the City centre would support the provision of at least 70,100 sq m of retail A1 – A5 use (Coventry AAP, paragraph 21). The retail strategy aims to maximise flexibility by grouping retail need within a broader use class range (A1 – A5) to ensure floor space can adapt to market needs quickly (Coventry AAP, paragraph 26). The addition of the word "based" after "retail" in Policy CC12 clarifies that other supporting uses within A1 - A5 would be acceptable in principle, providing additional flexibility (Coventry AAP, paragraph 27).

Exp08\nCombined.answer:
The Coventry Local Plan's approach to restricting hot food takeaways in specific city centre streets and encouraging healthier food options is outlined in Policy R6, which states that "Outlets should be located in defined centres" (Coventry Local Plan, Policy R6). The Hot Food Takeaway SPD provides further detail to this policy, stating that hot food takeaway applications will not be approved if they fall within a 5-minute walk from the gate(s) of any primary or secondary school, unless they are within a defined centre (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Section 4.2). In defined centres, provision must be made to minimise the negative impact on health and wellbeing, which may include conditions being applied relating to the opening hours of the hot food takeaway (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Section 4.2).

The NPPF's policy on achieving healthy, inclusive, and safe places is referenced in Chapter 8, which states that "planning policies and decisions should aim to achieve healthy, inclusive and safe places" (NPPF, Chapter 8). Paragraph 91c) within Chapter 8 refers specifically to the food environment, stating that planning policies should "enable and support healthy lifestyles, especially where this would address identified local health and well-being needs – for example through…access to healthier food…" (NPPF, Paragraph 91c).

The Coventry Local Plan's approach is consistent with the NPPF's policy, as it seeks to balance the requirements around economy with those around healthy communities (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2, Consultation Statement). The SPD does not seek to restrict all new hot food takeaway applications, but those that are likely to have the greatest negative impact on the health of the community (Hot Food Takeaway SPD, Appendix 2, Consultation Statement).

matches.text: 1 2 Introduction Coventry enjoys a rich history of architectural innovation and continual development, the city enjoys an environment where markedly different periods of development and associated architectural styles may be experienced in close proximity, thus delivering a highly legible built form narrative to the city. In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Paragraph 130 sets out how planning policy and decisions should ensure that development: a) will function well and add to the overall quality of the area, not just for the short term but over the lifetime of the development; b) are visually attractive as a result of good architecture, layout and appropriate and effective landscaping; c) are sympathetic to local character and history, including the surrounding built environment and landscape setting, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change (such as increased densities); d) establish or maintain a strong sense of place, using the arrangement of streets, spaces, building types and materials to create attractive, welcoming and distinctive places to live, work and visit; e) optimise the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development (including green and other public space) and support local facilities and transport networks; and f) create places that are safe, inclusive and accessible and which promote health and wellbeing, with a high standard of amenity for existing and future users; and where crime and disorder, and the fear of crime, do not undermine the quality of life or community cohesion and resilience. The NPPF further requires that the greatest possible amount of clarity on what is expected with respect to design outcomes and requirements is facilitated as early as possible in the development process (para 128). The Coventry Local Plan's Policy GE1 emphasizes integrating green infrastructure and high-quality design to improve air quality, noise, and neighbourhood amenity (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1). This policy requires new development proposals to make provision for green infrastructure, ensuring that development is integrated into the landscape and contributes to improvements in connectivity, biodiversity, and public access (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1, point 2). The NPPF requires planning policies to ensure that development is visually attractive, sympathetic to local character, and optimizes the potential of the site to accommodate development while supporting local facilities and transport networks (NPPF, paragraph 130). The NPPF also promotes the use of design guides and codes to create a framework setting design standards and requirements (NPPF, paragraph 128). The Coventry Local Plan's emphasis on green infrastructure aligns with the NPPF's requirements for sustainable development and protecting local amenity (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1; NPPF, paragraph 130). Article 4 directions are not directly mentioned in the provided sources, but the NPPF does discuss the importance of plan-making in protecting local amenity (NPPF, paragraph 130). The Coventry Local Plan's approach to green infrastructure is expected to improve air quality, reduce noise impacts, and enhance neighbourhood amenity, which is in line with the NPPF's objectives for sustainable development (Coventry Local Plan, Policy GE1; NPPF, paragraph 130).

Supplementary Planning Documents are subject to supporting evidence and consultation but are not publicly examined or subject to Sustainability Appraisal. As such, their ‘material weight’ in planning terms is less than that of a Local Plan, Area Action Plan or other Development Plan Document. Notwithstanding this, SPD’s must be adopted by a resolution of the Local Planning Authority and they are still important planning policy documents that provide technical guidance and supporting information to those submitting planning applications. A SPD does not introduce new policy, instead it builds and expands upon policies set out in the higher level plan (in this case the new Local Plan) to ensure they are interpreted and delivered in the most efficient and effective way. 6. matches.text: 1 2 Introduction Coventry enjoys a rich history of architectural innovation and continual development, the city enjoys an environment where markedly different periods of development and associated architectural styles may be experienced in close proximity, thus delivering a highly legible built form narrative to the city. In seeking to both respect these markers of development periods and also continually evolve as a city, the creative role of urban design in the built environment is critical in delivering positive environments which benefit the wellbeing of the city, contribute positively toward the challenge of the changing climate, attract inward investment, whilst also responding positively to established built form precedents which are a key marker of the cities identity. Plans, Policies and Programmes The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) 2021 and National Planning Practice Guidance (NPPG) which supplements the NPPF, places significant weight on good design as a means of bringing about sustainable development, creating better places, and delivering development which is suitable and appropriate for the communities where it takes place. Paragraph 130 sets out how planning policy and decisions should ensure that development: a) will function well and add to the overall quality of the area, not just for the short term but over the lifetime of the development; b) are visually attractive as a result of good architecture, layout and appropriate and effective landscaping; c) are sympathetic to local character and history, including the surrounding built environment and landscape setting, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change (such as increased densities); d) establish or maintain a strong sense of place, using the arrangement of streets, spaces, building types and materials to create attractive, welcoming and distinctive places to live, work and visit; e) optimise the potential of the site to accommodate and sustain an appropriate amount and mix of development (including green and other public space) and support local facilities and transport networks; and f) create places that are safe, inclusive and accessible and which promote health and wellbeing, with a high standard of amenity for existing and future users; and where crime and disorder, and the fear of crime, do not undermine the quality of life or community cohesion and resilience. The NPPF further requires that the greatest possible amount of clarity on what is expected with respect to design outcomes and requirements is facilitated as early as possible in the development process (para 128). It promotes the use of tools such as design guides and codes within instruments including local plans and supplementary planning documents to create a 3 framework setting design standards and requirements, with the level of detail or prescription tailored to the specific setting. Exp08\nCombined.answer:
Coventry's approach to addressing health inequalities, particularly in deprived areas, is to work collaboratively with various organisations to create healthy communities through planning policy (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 3.2). The city aims to reduce health inequalities by promoting healthy lifestyles, creating safe and inclusive living environments, and delivering community facilities (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 3.6). This approach is aligned with the national policy requirement for residential developments to create well-designed, attractive, and healthy places with efficient use of land, as stated in the NPPF (NPPF, paragraph 130). The NPPF requires that development should create places that are safe, inclusive, and accessible, and promote health and wellbeing (NPPF, paragraph 130). Coventry's Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan will have a significant influence on the physical development of the city over the next 15 years, and it is crucial to ensure that development impacts positively on the health of Coventry citizens (Coventry Local Plan Health Impact Assessment, Section 3.5).
